item.title: The Platero Brief, No. 37: Sunday, August 2, 2026
item.content:encoded:
Executive Pulse

#Macro signal

A US federal pre-release review for frontier AI models: The White House has been finalizing a voluntary framework with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google giving federal agencies up to 30 days to review the national-security implications of a new frontier model before public release, with the evaluation benchmarks kept classified. Meta is notably not part of it. Why it matters strategically: the largest AI vendors are now co-writing a regulatory threshold that any rival must clear to launch, which converts a compliance step into a competitive moat. Any leader who depends on frontier models should assume release timing is now partly a government variable, and plan roadmaps with that latency built in.

#Tech industry

  • Equity-funded compute (Anthropic/AMD, ~$5B in AMD equity for up to 2GW): Strategic implication: capital and supply are fusing. When your compute supplier is also your shareholder, the arm's-length vendor relationship that procurement is built to manage stops existing. Boards should ask where else their critical supply chain is quietly becoming an equity relationship.

#AI at the leadership level

The evidence this year points one direction: adoption is no longer the hard part, organizational adaptation is. Multi-year enterprise studies now find that structures are flattening as AI absorbs routine execution, and some firms are merging technology and people-leadership functions so systems and workforce design evolve together. The governance gap is the risk: a large majority of organizations report that AI governance is not keeping pace with how employees already use the tools. The leadership job is shifting from "buy the capability" to "redesign the org around it and govern it faster than staff can outrun you."

#Question worth asking your team this week

Where in our operation has AI already changed how the work gets done, without anyone changing who's accountable when it goes wrong? Find one such spot and assign the accountability before an incident does it for you.

Practitioner Pulse

#Try this now

  • Move one workflow from single-agent to orchestrator + critic: The pattern crystallizing across practitioner writing this year is decompose → specialize → critique: an orchestrator breaks a task into parts, specialized agents handle each, and a separate critic agent synthesizes and checks the result before it ships. You don't need a framework to try it. Take one prompt you run repeatedly (a competitive teardown, a brief QA, a data pull) and split it into a "do the work" pass and a distinct "find what's wrong with this" pass. The second pass catches the plausible-but-wrong output that a single run ships unchecked. Worth 20 minutes because it's the cheapest quality lift available on work you already automate.
  • Stop hand-tuning prompts; store representative examples instead: Practitioner consensus this year is that a few well-chosen, representative examples beat generic instructions and burn fewer tokens doing it. Instead of another paragraph of instruction telling the model what "good" looks like, paste two real examples of good output. For any recurring content or classification task, build a small library of 3-5 gold examples and rotate them in. It's faster to maintain than prose and it generalizes better.

#Case study worth stealing

Vendasta, autonomous "AI Employees" for SMB presence: On July 29 Vendasta shipped two GA agents, an AI Social Media Manager and an AI Blogger, aimed at small businesses that need a constant search and social footprint but have nobody to run it. The tactic worth stealing isn't the product, it's the packaging: they named the agents by the job title they replace, not the technology they use. For any digital team rolling out internal AI tooling, framing a tool as "the analyst that never sleeps" rather than "our new LLM workflow" changes adoption. People delegate to a role; they audit a technology.

#Framework or mental model

Orchestrator-worker-critic: A three-role split for any agentic task. The orchestrator owns decomposition and never does the work itself; workers are narrow and interchangeable; the critic's only job is to try to break the workers' output. The insight for digital leaders is that the critic is the role teams skip, and it's the one that separates a demo from something you'd put in front of a customer. Apply it to human workflows too: the person who scoped the work should not be the person who signs off on it.

AI Stack Daily

#Vendor & platform moves

  • Anthropic × AMD: Anthropic closed a capacity agreement for up to 2 gigawatts of MI450/Helios-generation compute, a deal reported to include up to $5B in AMD equity, landing the same week as AMD's Advancing AI 2026 launch of the Helios/MI400 platform. Signal: the model labs are now diversifying off a single silicon supplier and paying for it with equity, not just cash. For anyone building a stack, single-vendor compute risk is now a board-level concern one layer down from where you buy.
  • Vendasta ships autonomous "AI Employees" to GA (Jul 29): An AI Social Media Manager and AI Blogger, sold to SMBs as headcount, not software. Signal: the martech mid-market is repackaging agents as roles. Expect suite vendors to follow with "AI SDR / AI analyst" SKUs priced per-seat-replaced rather than per-seat.

#Category watch

Agentic martech (autonomous execution layer): The category is shifting from AI that drafts to AI that runs the task end to end, most visibly in social, content, and SMB campaign management. The players splitting the field are the horizontal labs (selling raw capability) and the vertical suites (selling the finished job with guardrails). For a martech org-builder the buying question is changing from "does it have AI" to "how much of the loop does it close, and who owns the failure when it closes it wrong."

#Stack intelligence

The consolidation-vs-best-of-breed pendulum is being reset by agents. When execution moves inside an agent, the integration cost that used to justify buying one suite drops, because the agent brokers between tools. That quietly favors best-of-breed again for teams that can run their own orchestration, and favors the suite for teams that can't. The practical read: your ability to own an orchestration layer is now the variable that decides whether suite lock-in is worth paying for.

#Foundations concept of the day

Clean rooms: A clean room is a secure, neutral environment where two parties (say a retailer and a brand) match and analyze their customer data together without either side handing over the raw records. Each uploads encrypted data; the room returns aggregate results (overlap, incrementality, audience size) but never lets one party export the other's individuals. It matters at scale because it's the compromise that keeps first-party data useful in a privacy-restricted, cookieless world, retail media networks run on it. Real example: a grocery chain and a CPG brand measuring whether an ad campaign actually drove in-store purchases, without the grocer exposing its loyalty file.

#Watch list

  • Equity-for-compute deals as a pattern: if labs keep paying for chips with stock, chipmakers become quasi-investors in their own customers, a structural entanglement worth tracking for how it distorts competitive dynamics.

Markets Signal

#Macro pulse

Weekend, markets closed. Reading off Friday's (Jul 31) US close: S&P 500 +0.7% to ~7,489, Dow +0.5% to ~52,485, with the Dow posting a fourth straight winning month on an Amazon-led surge. The wrinkle for airline cost structures: WTI crude climbed to ~$84.67/bbl (+1.3% on the day), and rising oil is now the market's live inflation worry, meaning fuel input costs and rate-cut timing are pulling in opposite directions heading into August.

#AI infrastructure watch

The capacity story is now the compute story. Anthropic's up-to-2GW AMD deal (with ~$5B in AMD equity) and continued reports of Nvidia-backed multi-gigawatt data-center projects confirm the constraint has moved from chips alone to chips + power. Nuclear-powered, near-waterless data centers (the Valar Atomics/Nvidia micro-reactor demo, Nvidia's DSX water-efficient design) are the tell: energy and cooling, not silicon, are becoming the binding limit on what AI can scale to in 12-18 months.

#Signal or noise?

Signal. Equity-for-compute and power-first data-center design are structural, not one-week moves, they reprice the whole AI supply chain.

#Watch tomorrow

Monday's open and whether the oil bid holds, a sustained crude move above the mid-$80s pressures both airline margins and the inflation read that sets rate expectations.

item.title: The Platero Brief, No. 36: Saturday, August 1, 2026
item.content:encoded:
Executive Pulse

#Macro signal

Risk-on close to July, oil the outlier: US indexes finished the last session of July markedly higher, with the S&P 500 up 0.7% and the Dow booking a fourth straight winning month, as investors looked past rising bond yields on the strength of megacap earnings. The dissonant note is crude, with WTI up nearly 4% on the day to roughly $87. For leaders, the signal is a market comfortable paying up for AI and consumer strength while energy costs quietly reintroduce input-cost risk. Plan for a second half where demand looks fine but margins face a fuel and rates squeeze.

#Tech industry

  • Enterprise AI's "platform moment": Industry analysis this week frames a shift from scattered AI tools to governed "systems of intelligence" tied directly to business outcomes. Strategic implication: the buying decision is moving up from individual tool procurement to platform and governance choices made at the executive level. The window for letting teams adopt AI point solutions bottom-up is closing, because the cleanup cost is now visible on the balance sheet.

#AI at the leadership level

The governance bill for two years of bottom-up AI adoption is coming due. Fresh survey data has 67% of executives believing their company has already suffered a data leak from an employee using an unapproved AI tool, 55% describing internal AI use as a "chaotic free-for-all," and 79% saying AI apps are being built in silos. Meanwhile only 29% see significant ROI from generative AI and 23% from AI agents. The pattern is a direct governance failure, not a technology one. Sprawl without a control layer produces both the security exposure and the weak returns. Expect the Chief Data and AI Officer mandate to harden from evangelism to control, and expect boards to start asking who owns the AI risk register.

#Leadership & org design

IRIS Software Group appointed its first Chief Data and AI Officer this week to lead global data strategy, a responsible-AI framework, and enterprise governance under a single role. The structural move worth noting is the consolidation of data strategy and AI governance into one accountable seat rather than splitting them across a CDO and a separate AI function. For org-builders, the lesson is that a fragmented AI mandate is what produced the silo-and-leak problem above. One accountable owner with authority over both the data layer and the AI policy is the emerging fix.

#Question worth asking your team this week

If an auditor asked us today to list every AI tool touching customer or proprietary data, who owns each one, and what data it can reach, could we answer in an hour? If not, that gap is our real AI strategy right now.

Practitioner Pulse

#Try this now

  • Codex Remote, now GA on ChatGPT plans: OpenAI moved Codex Remote and workspace agents to general availability this week, with new admin controls over how agents run inside Business, Enterprise, and Edu. The practical unlock: you can hand an agent a scoped task, let it run remotely against a repo or workspace, and review the output as a diff rather than babysitting a chat. Worth 20 minutes to test on one real backlog task and see where it lands versus where you still need to intervene.
  • Vertesia Studio Assistant: An agentic assistant embedded inside the builder that writes prompts, tests the same task across different models, learns from execution, then refines and publishes the agent. This is the emerging shape of prompt work: you stop hand-tuning a single prompt and instead let the tool run the model bake-off for you. Even if you never adopt Vertesia, the pattern is the point. Treat prompts as tested, versioned assets, not one-off strings.
  • BridgeApp orchestration layer: Launched July 27, it connects people, agents, tasks, and context in one workspace and is built to move a work item from to-do to finished pull request without tool switching. The idea worth stealing regardless of vendor: the friction in agent workflows is now the handoffs between tools, not the model. Map where your team loses context between systems before you buy anything.

#Case study worth stealing

Akeneo, Agentic Ziggy inside the Product Cloud: Akeneo shipped an agentic orchestration layer that coordinates specialist agents for data modeling, schema mapping, enrichment, and continuous quality checks on product data. Rather than one general agent trying to do everything, they assigned narrow agents to narrow jobs and put a coordinator on top. Any team drowning in product or catalog data can adapt the structure. Decompose the messy job into specialist steps, give each step a checkable output, and orchestrate rather than automate end to end. The quality-check agent running continuously is the detail most teams skip.

#Framework or mental model

Orchestration over autonomy: The through-line across this week's releases (Vertesia's Process Engine, BridgeApp, Akeneo) is a deliberate middle ground between fully autonomous agents and rigid deterministic automation. Autonomous agents are hard to trust and hard to debug. Rigid automation cannot handle variance. Orchestration defines the process as a diagram or spec, then lets agents fill the steps under supervision. For digital leaders, the takeaway is to stop asking "can an agent do this whole job" and start asking "what is the smallest process I can define and hand to supervised agents this quarter."

AI Stack Daily

#Vendor & platform moves

  • Everseen acquires the Viztel portfolio from RadiusAI: Extends Everseen's Vision AI platform from the checkout lane to the entire store floor. Signal: retail computer-vision is consolidating from point solutions (loss prevention at the till) into full-store sensing platforms. The buyers want one vendor covering the whole physical funnel, not a stitched-together set of cameras.
  • Edge226 completes acquisition of AnyClip: Merges video content processing with performance advertising. Signal: the video and performance-ad stacks are collapsing into each other. As creative becomes machine-generated and machine-optimized, owning both the content pipeline and the buying engine is becoming one capability rather than two vendors.
  • ActiveCampaign ships a Google Ads connector for Active Intelligence: Marketers can now push ActiveCampaign data into Google Ads and launch Performance Max campaigns from inside ActiveCampaign. Signal: the mid-market automation platforms are racing to become the single console for owned and paid, not just email. The CRM is trying to eat the ad-buying seat.

#Category watch

Agentic commerce infrastructure: Algolia enhanced its Agent Studio for building and optimizing onsite agentic commerce experiences the same week Akeneo shipped an agentic layer over product data. The category forming here is the plumbing beneath AI shopping agents: search, product data quality, and agent orchestration as a connected stack. The players are the search and PIM vendors repositioning fast, and the bet is that when shopping shifts from browsing to delegated agents, whoever owns clean product data and the retrieval layer owns the transaction.

#Stack intelligence

The consolidation pattern this week is vertical, not horizontal. Vendors are not buying competitors for scale, they are buying up and down their own value chain (checkout to full store, content to ad buying, CRM to paid media). For anyone building a martech org, the practical read is that the "best of breed versus suite" question is reopening. The suites are re-absorbing the adjacent point solutions, and the integration tax you pay for best-of-breed is rising as each vendor tries to own more of the flow.

#Foundations concept of the day

Product Information Management (PIM): A PIM is the system of record for everything you know about a product, its attributes, descriptions, images, specs, pricing rules, and channel-specific variants, kept clean and consistent so it can flow to every place the product appears. It matters at scale because a retailer with a hundred thousand SKUs across a website, marketplaces, and retail-media placements cannot manually keep each listing correct. Real example: a consumer-electronics brand selling on its own site plus Amazon plus a retailer's app uses a PIM so a single spec change (say a revised battery rating) propagates everywhere at once. This is why the agentic-commerce vendors are converging on product data. AI shopping agents are only as trustworthy as the PIM feeding them.

#Watch list

  • CRM platforms moving into ad buying: ActiveCampaign's Performance Max integration is a small move that signals a large one. Watch whether the larger CRM and marketing clouds follow, because owning the paid-media seat from inside the CRM changes the buying center for ad budgets.
  • Retail vision platforms: With Everseen consolidating full-store sensing, watch which grocery and big-box retailers standardize on a single vision vendor. That decision sets the data layer for in-store retail media next.

Markets Signal

#Macro pulse

  • Canada: The S&P/TSX Composite closed 35,226.14, down 279.70 (-0.79%), dragged by weak mining shares as gold fell and by a sharp Telus drop after the telecom cut its full-year outlook. USD/CAD near flat at 1.4013, keeping the loonie soft around the 1.40 handle, which supports Canadian carrier costs on domestic spend but raises the bill on USD-denominated fuel and aircraft.
  • USA: Indexes closed the last session of July higher. S&P 500 +0.7% to 7,489.72, Nasdaq +1% to 25,373.85, Dow +276.97 (+0.53%) to 52,485.03, with the Dow posting a fourth straight winning month. Amazon surged on earnings, and the tape looked past rising bond yields.
  • Asia: Nikkei 225 jumped 4.03% to 64,362.02, a standout move, with Shanghai Composite +0.72% and Hang Seng roughly flat at +0.10%.
  • Oil: WTI crude spiked to about $86.80, up 3.84% on the day. This clears the 2% flag and matters directly to airline margins. A move of this size on jet fuel input costs offsets a meaningful slice of a strong demand quarter.

#Today's industry move

Two vertical-integration deals closed in the martech and vision stack. Everseen acquired the Viztel portfolio from RadiusAI to extend retail computer vision from the checkout lane to the full store, and Edge226 completed its acquisition of AnyClip, merging video content processing with performance advertising. Both are consolidation up the value chain rather than for scale.

#AI infrastructure watch

The nuclear-for-AI thread continues to firm up. Nvidia and Valar Atomics are progressing a nearly waterless, roughly 30-megawatt AI data center in Utah powered by a small modular reactor, after demonstrating Blackwell chips running on the microreactor live. The constraint shaping AI two years out is not chips, it is power and water, and the hyperscalers are now solving for both at the site level.

#Signal or noise?

The oil spike is the signal to watch. One day is a blip, but a nearly 4% move into a quarter where airlines are otherwise seeing strong demand is the kind of input-cost pressure that compounds if it holds.

#Watch tomorrow

Whether crude holds above $85 into the new week. If it does, it reframes the airline margin story from demand-led optimism to a cost-side squeeze, and it will show up in carrier and travel-name sentiment first.

item.title: The Platero Brief, No. 35: Friday, July 31, 2026
item.content:encoded:
Executive Pulse

#Macro signal

Stagflation risk moves from talk to data. The Fed held rates at 3.5-3.75% on Wednesday, but with three of twelve FOMC members dissenting in favor of a hike, the split itself is the story. Q2 GDP came in at a 1.5% annual rate, down from 2.1% and below the 1.8% consensus, while PCE inflation is still running 3.7% year over year. Slowing growth with sticky prices is the setup the Fed has no clean tool for. The Dow fell 2.2% on the decision, its worst day since April 2025, and 30-year yields pushed above 5.2%. Strategically, the era of assuming rate cuts will bail out weak demand is over. Leaders planning 2027 budgets should model a scenario where capital stays expensive and top-line growth is soft at the same time. That kills the "grow into it" logic behind a lot of AI capex and headcount plans, and rewards teams that can show margin, not just momentum.

#Tech industry

  • Microsoft now sells implementation as the product. Microsoft stood up Frontier Company, a $2.5B subsidiary with roughly 6,000 engineers and specialists embedded directly inside enterprise clients (LSEG, Unilever, Land O'Lakes, Accenture) to deploy and optimize AI systems, and notably to help customers pick the best model mix whether it comes from Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or open source. The strategic signal: the hyperscalers have concluded the bottleneck is no longer model access, it is making models useful inside messy real companies. The margin is moving from the model to the deployment. Every vendor pitching you a platform is quietly discovering the money is in the services layer they said you would not need.
  • AI agents cross into production, and so does the risk number. Major platforms shipped agent frameworks trustworthy enough for narrow jobs (invoice processing, customer triage, data entry), moving AI from answering questions to completing work. Gartner attached a figure to the downside: $234B in enterprise software spend is now at risk from agentic AI displacing incumbent tools. The implication for boards is that your existing SaaS stack is no longer a safe default line item. Agents don't just automate labor, they collapse whole categories of software you currently pay seat licenses for.

#AI at the leadership level

The gap on AI is now inside the boardroom, not between the company and the market. BCG's 2026 survey of 625 CEOs and board members found 35% of CEOs think their boards overestimate what AI can replace, while 60% of CEOs think their boards are too impatient with the pace of transformation. The tell is cadence: only 26% of boards discuss AI at every meeting, but among companies reporting strong AI returns, 63% put it on every agenda. AI performance is tracking governance rhythm, not budget size. If AI is a quarterly update in your boardroom, you are already structurally behind the firms that treat it as a standing agenda item.

#Leadership & org design

The consulting model is being restructured by the tool it sells. McKinsey is cutting roughly 10% of staff, concentrated in back-office, junior research, and practice areas where generative AI has compressed delivery timelines, with work that once took analyst teams now done in hours. The durable lesson for any org builder: the leverage is shifting from headcount to a smaller number of people who can operate AI as a force multiplier. The relevant design question is no longer "how many analysts," it is "how few operators, each amplified." Firms whose economics depend on billing junior hours by the head are watching their own product commoditize their staffing model.

#Question worth asking your team this week

If capital stays expensive and demand stays soft through 2027, which of our current AI investments still pays for itself on margin alone, without assuming faster growth to justify it?

Practitioner Pulse

#Try this now

  • LinkedIn Campaign Manager AI creative suite (Ads Personalization + AI Variants): LinkedIn's July creative tools resurfaced this week with hard numbers. Campaigns running five or more ad variants saw over 20% higher CTR, and Ads Personalization (tailoring by job title, company, industry) lifted CTR 1.4 points on website conversion and 2.4 points on video lead-gen for SMB advertisers. This week, take one live campaign, load your fonts, colors, and tone into Brand Kit so the AI stays on-brand, then spin up five variants instead of one. Worth 20 minutes because it removes the "we only have bandwidth for one creative" excuse that caps most B2B ad performance. Caveat: LinkedIn has not published sample size or method behind the 20% figure, so treat it as a hypothesis to A/B, not a guarantee.
  • Plain-English AI evals you own, not approve: The reframe landing across product teams this month is that the PM owns the eval, not just signs off on it. Write evals as four plain-English parts: role, context, goal, and labels (pass/fail criteria), no code required. Pick the single AI feature you shipped last quarter, write 20 real user inputs, and score the outputs yourself against those labels before your next release. Worth 20 minutes because user tolerance for generic AI output has cratered, and an eval set is the only way to catch quality regressions before customers do.
  • A persistent context workspace before any AI workflow: The foundational move under evals, agents, and prototyping is a shared workspace (Claude Projects, Google Gems, ChatGPT Projects, Copilot Studio) that holds your personas, constraints, brand rules, and metric definitions. Spend 20 minutes loading yours once, and every downstream prompt stops starting from zero. This is the difference between AI that guesses about your product and AI that reasons from your actual context.

#Case study worth stealing

Netflix and Adidas, dynamic creative optimization via Cortex: The two brands partnered with AI marketing platform Cortex to serve personalized ad creative built from viewing history, past purchase data, and contextual signals rather than one fixed asset per audience. Instead of a designer hand-building a handful of variants, the system assembles and targets creative per viewer against real behavioral inputs. The steal for loyalty and travel teams: your CRM already holds the behavioral signal (trips booked, tier, dwell time, cart) that most brands still ignore at the creative layer. Wire that signal into creative assembly, not just audience selection, and you personalize the "what and why," not only the "who."

#Framework or mental model

AI-first, not AI-only: This month Klarna, Duolingo, and Shopify all walked back aggressive "AI-first" claims after automation underdelivered, with Klarna resuming human hiring when its chatbot's lower-quality responses hurt satisfaction. The usable model that replaces the hype: map one messy process end to end, insert AI where it removes toil, keep a human review gate, and prove time saved or errors reduced before scaling. Digital leaders should apply it to the loudest automation ask in their org right now by scoping it to a single workflow with a measured before-and-after, instead of an org-wide "AI-first" mandate that has no baseline to defend.

#Rabbit hole

Agentic commerce is quietly rewriting the top of the funnel. AI-referred shoppers converted 31% higher over the 2025 holidays (Adobe Analytics), AI-driven orders grew roughly 15x from January 2025 to January 2026, and AI platforms are projected to drive around $20.9 billion in US retail spend this year, nearly four times 2025. Salesforce's July B2C Commerce release added Agentic Commerce Search and native OpenAI feed distribution so a storefront's catalog stays accurate inside ChatGPT. The practitioner question worth an afternoon: is your product, rate, or inventory data structured and fresh enough for an agent to read and transact against, or are you invisible the moment a customer shops through an assistant instead of your homepage?

AI Stack Daily

#Vendor & platform moves

  • OpenAI + The Trade Desk: Reports this week (via The Information) surfaced early talks for OpenAI to lean on The Trade Desk to automate and scale ad sales inside ChatGPT, as OpenAI projects advertising could roughly double consumer ChatGPT revenue toward $17B this year. TTD stock rallied on the news. Signal: The next demand surface is the chat interface, and even a would-be walled garden with $25B in revenue is choosing to rent programmatic plumbing rather than build a full ad stack from scratch. Buy-side infrastructure keeps its relevance precisely as AI threatens to disintermediate it.
  • Walmart / Vibe.co: Walmart is absorbing self-serve CTV platform Vibe.co (reported near $1.2B, expected to close by end of FY2027) and folding it into Walmart Connect. Vibe lets a mid-market advertiser launch live TV campaigns in under five minutes from $50/day. Signal: Retail media, connected TV, and SMB self-service are collapsing into one motion. The moat is first-party purchase data from 150M+ customers wired directly into CTV targeting and closed-loop sales attribution, which is something a pure DSP cannot replicate.
  • MoEngage: The engagement platform raised $100M (Goldman Sachs Alternatives, A91 Partners) to scale its Merlin AI agent suite, then followed with roughly $180M more weeks later. Signal: Capital is flowing to the agentic execution layer that sits on top of customer data, not to another system of record. The bet is that orchestration and next-best-action, not storage, is where marketing value concentrates next.

#Category watch

The CDP is splitting in two. The category is bifurcating into martech CDPs built for internal lifecycle orchestration (Adobe, Hightouch, Zeotap) and adtech CDPs, increasingly rebranded as collaborative audience platforms, built for privacy-first activation across the ad ecosystem (Decentriq, Permutive, Mediarithmics). If you are building a martech org, this ends the era of buying one CDP to do everything. You now make a deliberate call about whether your primary need is orchestration inside your own funnel or safe audience collaboration with partners and publishers, because the tooling for those two jobs is diverging fast.

#Stack intelligence

Warehouse-native is winning the architecture argument. Composable and warehouse-native CDP vendors grew headcount 7.8% against a 1.3% industry average, roughly 6x, which is where talent votes with its feet. The emerging pattern: keep the customer data in the warehouse (Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery) as the single source of truth, then layer activation and increasingly agentic next-best-action on top rather than copying data into a monolithic suite. Databricks entering with an agentic CDP validates the direction. The buy-vs-build line has moved: buy the activation and agent layer, own the data layer, and stop paying a suite vendor to hold a second copy of data you already store.

#Foundations concept of the day

Data clean rooms. A clean room is a secure environment where two parties (say a brand and a retailer, or an advertiser and a publisher) can match and analyze their customer data together without either side seeing or exporting the other's raw records. Instead of handing over a customer list, each party loads data into a neutral space that only permits aggregated, privacy-safe outputs: overlap counts, audience segments, campaign measurement. It matters at scale because third-party cookies and device IDs are decaying, regulation is tightening, and the richest data now sits locked inside walled gardens and retailers. Clean rooms are how first-party data gets combined without the legal and privacy exposure of moving it. Amazon Marketing Cloud is the canonical example: advertisers run analytics across pseudonymized Amazon signals plus their own inputs and never touch the underlying rows. AWS Clean Rooms and Snowflake now support cross-cloud collaboration with zero data movement, so a travel brand, a bank, and a media network can measure a shared campaign without any of them exposing a customer file.

#Watch list

  • The agentic CDP. Databricks and MoEngage's Merlin are early signals that the CDP conversation is shifting from where data lives to what autonomously acts on it. Watch whether these move past pilot stage. BCG's CMO survey found 96% say AI is transforming marketing but only 8% run genuinely multi-agent autonomous campaigns. The gap between narrative and production is the real signal to track.
  • AI chat as an ad surface. If the OpenAI and Trade Desk talks mature, conversational interfaces become a new inventory type with no cookies, no page, and a very different attention model. Anyone building a media plan should start asking what a "placement" even means inside a chatbot.

Markets Signal

#Macro pulse

Canada: TSX closed near 35,506 (+0.49%), lifted by banks and gold miners. USD/CAD sits around 1.40, with the loonie firm after the Fed held rates this week, up from a 1.42 low on Monday. A stronger CAD trims the domestic value of USD-denominated international fares for Canadian carriers. USA: Records again. S&P 500 +0.67% and Nasdaq +1.32% to fresh highs, Dow +0.38%. Amazon's blowout quarter carried tech higher, while Apple fell on a soft forward outlook and rising component costs. Asia: Broadly green. Shanghai Composite +0.76% to ~3,834 on stimulus hopes, Nikkei 225 +0.71% near 61,867, Hang Seng roughly flat +0.20%. Oil: WTI quiet near $84, off about 0.5%. No margin signal for airlines today.

#Today's industry move

Amazon's Q2 reset the cloud narrative. AWS grew 37% year over year to $42.2B, its fastest since 2021 and well past the ~31% Street expectation, now at a $169B annualized run rate. AI and custom-chip businesses each cleared $25B run rates growing triple digits. Management said even at raised spend it still cannot meet all 2026 demand, and expects the same in 2027. The read for travel and loyalty leaders: cloud reacceleration means the AI capacity crunch is a demand story, not a hype story, and compute pricing power stays with the hyperscalers.

#AI infrastructure watch

The tell was in the capex line. Amazon lifted 2026 cash capex to about $220B from roughly $200B, and named higher memory cost as the driver, on top of data centers, networking, and AI chips. Memory is emerging as the new bottleneck in the stack, ahead of raw GPU supply. When a hyperscaler raises a $200B budget by 10% mid-year and points at DRAM and HBM pricing, that pressure flows downstream to every buyer of AI-heavy SaaS.

#Signal or noise?

Signal. This is the AI capex supercycle broadening from GPUs into memory and power, with cloud demand outrunning supply into 2027.

#Watch tomorrow

Whether the memory-cost flag in Amazon's guide shows up in other hyperscaler and chip commentary, and whether USD/CAD holds sub-1.41 into next week's data.

item.title: The Platero Brief, No. 34: Thursday, July 30, 2026
item.content:encoded:
Executive Pulse

#Macro signal

The rate-cut story is dead. Plan for the hike. The Fed held at 3.50 to 3.75 percent yesterday, but the vote was a fractured 9 to 3, and the three dissenters wanted to raise, not cut. That is the real headline. A renewed Iran war and the disruption around the Strait of Hormuz have pushed crude above 80 dollars and reintroduced an energy-driven inflation shock, and futures now price a 72 percent chance of a quarter-point hike in September. Equities read it correctly: the Dow fell more than 2 percent on the day. For the past year most planning assumptions have quietly baked in falling rates and cheaper capital arriving by Q4. Strip that out. The strategic implication is to re-underwrite every 2026 and 2027 investment case against flat-to-rising cost of capital and a live geopolitical energy premium. Deals, hiring plans, and capex that only clear the bar in a cutting cycle should be flagged now, not in September.

#Tech industry

  • AI agents move from free demo to metered line item. Major platforms began billing for autonomous agents this month while positioning agent governance as the enterprise selling point, not the model itself. Strategic implication: agent spend is shifting from a science-project budget to a recurring per-action operating cost. Whoever in your org is spinning up agents is now creating consumption liabilities that scale with usage. Get agent cost and access under the same procurement and FinOps discipline as cloud before the bill compounds.
  • A cross-lab employee coalition asked Washington to build a coordinated slowdown mechanism. More than 1,100 staff across the leading AI labs signed a letter asking government to stand up the technical and governance infrastructure for a verifiable, coordinated pause if systems outrun oversight. It is not a call to stop today. It is a signal that regulatory friction on frontier AI is moving from hypothetical to structural, and that timeline risk now belongs on the board agenda for anyone betting the roadmap on the frontier curve staying unregulated.

#AI at the leadership level

The adoption-to-control gap is now the defining governance failure. Survey data this month puts roughly 96 percent of enterprises running AI agents in production while only about 12 percent say they can actually govern them. These agents hold persistent access to email, calendars, CRM, and internal APIs and act at machine speed, which makes them, in practice, non-human insiders with standing credentials. Point-in-time review before deployment does not touch this. The leadership shift underway is from pre-launch approval to continuous runtime enforcement, and the executive question is no longer "did we approve this model" but "who can see, throttle, and revoke every agent operating in our systems right now."

#Leadership & org design

The orgs closing the governance gap are doing it with explicit accountability tiers rather than a single AI owner. The pattern: data leaders own context and acceptable-risk policy, ML and platform teams own agent behavior and gateway controls, security owns audit, and the domain teams own data quality. The lesson for org design is that "AI governance" fails when it is one person's title and works when it is a named layer of ownership mapped to how the technology actually flows through the business. Centralize the policy, distribute the accountability.

#Question worth asking your team this week

If capital stays expensive and energy stays volatile through 2027, which of our current bets only make sense in the cheap-money world we were quietly assuming, and what do we cut or restructure first?

Practitioner Pulse

#Try this now

  • Run paid campaigns from inside your chat tool (PropellerAds MCP connector): A free MCP connector released this week lets you manage live ad campaigns directly from Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor. The API token stays local and grants scoped permissions for bids, budgets, targeting, and creative, so you can ask "pause the two worst-performing creatives and shift 20% of budget to the top format" in plain language instead of clicking through a dashboard. Worth 20 minutes to see whether your own ad or MarTech vendors now ship an MCP endpoint, because managing spend from the same window where you draft strategy collapses a real handoff.
  • Cyabra narrative-intelligence agent for brand and comms teams: Launched July 28, it returns a coordination assessment with a confidence score and a downloadable, shareable report in under 30 seconds, instead of a dashboard someone has to interpret and defend in a meeting. The transferable move for any team: judge agent outputs by whether they produce a defensible answer with a confidence level, not another chart to stare at. Point it at a suspected coordinated campaign or a spike in brand chatter and see if the explanation holds.
  • Diagnose "context rot" before adding more prompt: When an AI agent starts repeating itself, forgetting decisions it already made, or inventing tools that do not exist, the fix is almost never a longer prompt. It is a signal the context window is polluted. This week, when an agent misbehaves, first strip and reorganize what it can see rather than piling on instructions. That single reflex separates operators who scale AI from those who keep re-explaining themselves.

#Case study worth stealing

Dstillery and Canvas Worldwide, in-flight agentic campaign optimization: The two ran what they describe as the first live agentic optimization of a running programmatic campaign. Their DS-1 agent monitors performance continuously, flags which segments are outperforming, and recommends shifting budget toward them, replacing the weekly or monthly manual trader review with corrections that happen between reporting checkpoints. Traders keep approval authority, so the human stays on judgment and the agent handles the watching. Any digital team running always-on spend can adapt the pattern: let an agent surface underperformance in real time and route a recommendation to a human for sign-off, rather than waiting for the next scheduled report to notice waste.

#Framework or mental model

The Context Pyramid (four layers for any AI workflow): Structure everything an agent knows into four layers that update at different speeds. Identity (the system prompt: who the agent is, changed rarely), Knowledge (retrieval and stored facts, updated occasionally), State (recent history and current blockers, updated every turn), and Task (the goal and success criteria for right now, replaced each time). The operational companion is write, select, compress, isolate: write important context to files outside the window, select only what is needed now, compress history periodically, and isolate context by role so each agent sees only its slice. Digital leaders can apply it to move a team off clever one-off prompts and onto reusable workflows where quality does not depend on one person remembering the magic words.

AI Stack Daily

#Vendor & platform moves

  • Monetate acquires Simon AI: Announced today. Monetate, the on-site personalization vendor, is buying Simon AI, an agentic platform built on a warehouse-native composable CDP with a live unified profile, 100-plus channel integrations, and a prompt-driven interface that pulls real-world signals like inventory and weather. Terms undisclosed, paired with a growth-capital injection. Signal: the CDP market is consolidating around agents, not dashboards. On-site optimization vendors need omnichannel orchestration and a live profile to stay relevant, and buying an agentic CDP is now faster than building one. Expect more personalization and experience-optimization players to pair up with composable data layers over the next two quarters.
  • The Trade Desk loosens fees under Amazon DSP pressure: The dominant independent DSP is cutting fee flexibility for the first time in years as Amazon DSP's low costs and expanding off-site inventory pull cost-conscious buyers. Advertisers are keeping faith but shopping around, and 73 percent of enterprise advertisers already run three or more DSPs at once. Signal: the independent DSP's pricing power is eroding as the retail media giants use owned data and inventory, Amazon's Prime Video and retail intent, as a wedge. For anyone building a media stack, single-DSP dependence is now a risk, and multi-DSP orchestration is becoming the default architecture.
  • Holdcos trade AI infrastructure costs for principal media commitments: Agency holding companies are settling AI cost ambiguity by absorbing the AI infrastructure bill in exchange for brands committing predetermined volumes of principal inventory, media the holdco buys in bulk and resells at a markup. Signal: there is still no clean pricing model for agency AI, so agencies are folding it into the one lever they control, media arbitrage. This bundles a conflict of interest into the AI relationship. Leaders buying agency AI should price and contract the AI layer separately from media, or lose visibility into what they are actually paying for.

#Category watch

Agentic CDPs: The customer data platform is being rebuilt around autonomous agents in real time. In the last week alone Monetate bought Simon AI, BlueConic acquired Blueshift to add AI agents and actions to customer data, Databricks pushed CustomerLake to run the CDP directly on its data platform, and HubSpot expanded Breeze AI with tooling to build and govern agents. The center of gravity is shifting from unifying data for humans to query, toward a live warehouse-native profile that agents act on directly. The buyer question is moving from "which CDP" to "whose data platform does my CDP live on."

#Stack intelligence

The composable, warehouse-native pattern is winning the enterprise CDP debate. Rather than copying customer data into a standalone CDP, teams are increasingly building the profile on top of the data platform they already govern, Databricks, Snowflake, BigQuery, where identity, AI, and enterprise context already sit. This collapses the old copy-and-sync CDP into a query layer plus an activation layer, cuts data duplication and governance risk, and makes the "single customer view" a live view instead of a nightly batch. The trade-off is that it demands real data-engineering maturity, so the buy-versus-build line is moving: buy the activation and agent layer, build the profile on your existing warehouse.

#Foundations concept of the day

Data clean rooms: A clean room is a secure, neutral environment where two parties match and analyze their data together without either side seeing the other's raw records. A retailer and a brand can overlap loyalty and purchase data to measure whether an ad drove a sale, but neither walks away with the other's customer list. It works by matching on hashed identifiers and returning only aggregated, privacy-safe outputs, so no individual is exposed. This matters because third-party cookies are gone and walled gardens keep their data inside, so the clean room has become the connective tissue between purchase data, campaign measurement, and privacy compliance. It is the engine under retail media: a grocery chain, a bank running a card-linked offer program, or a streaming platform can each let advertisers measure real outcomes against first-party data without handing it over. Fewer than half of US retail media networks offer clean room capabilities today, which is exactly why the ones that do are pulling ahead.

#Watch list

  • Databricks CustomerLake: The clearest sign that the CDP is becoming a feature of the data platform rather than a product you buy beside it. If the warehouse vendors own the profile, standalone CDPs get squeezed toward the activation and agent layer.
  • Google Ads API passkey mandate (August 5): Google is forcing all Ads API access onto biometric or device-based passkeys with a seven-day trust window, aimed at agency account-takeover scams. Small in isolation, but a marker of security becoming a first-class constraint on martech operations, plan for the operational friction around staff turnover.

Markets Signal

#Macro pulse

The Fed drove everything this week. Wednesday's 9-3 hawkish hold (rate held at 3.5 to 3.75 percent, three regional presidents dissenting toward a hike) sent the Dow down 1,153 points to 51,594 and the S&P 500 off 1.52 percent. Thursday reversed hard on megacap earnings: S&P 500 back to 7,414 (up 1.34 percent), Nasdaq up 2.69 percent to 25,101, Dow up 0.66 percent. The tell underneath the rebound is the bond market, where the 30-year Treasury yield pushed to a multidecade high near 5.24 percent. Rates staying higher for longer is now the base case, with markets pricing two hikes into 2026.

Canada: the TSX fell 1.16 percent Wednesday to 35,334, dragged by the same Fed read and a rising oil tape. USD/CAD sits near 1.408 (loonie at 71.01 cents US), roughly flat and not a flag today. A weaker Canadian dollar modestly helps inbound international demand but raises USD-denominated fuel and lease costs for Canadian carriers.

Asia held up better than North America. Hang Seng closed up 1.96 percent at 25,808, Shanghai Composite up 0.40 percent at 3,828.

Oil is the macro flag. WTI trades near $84 and Brent pushed above $92 after fresh US airstrikes on Iranian targets and drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities. Crude is up more than 4 percent on the week. For airline planners this is a direct margin and hedging signal, and a jet fuel cost problem building in real time.

#Today's industry move

Microsoft is the story. The stock surged more than 11 percent after Azure cloud revenue topped $100 billion for the first time, validating that AI demand is converting into booked cloud consumption. Meta went the other way, down roughly 9 percent, after raising 2026 capex guidance to $125 to $145 billion for its superintelligence build without a clear near-term return on that spend. The split verdict is the whole market right now: investors will pay up for AI infrastructure that is already monetizing and punish AI infrastructure that is still a promise. Alphabet set the tone earlier in the week, beating on results but posting its first negative free cash flow as a public company on soaring capex.

#AI infrastructure watch

The capex numbers reframe the sector. Consensus 2026 hyperscaler capex is now near $682 billion, up roughly $300 billion year over year, with 2027 projected near $878 billion. That is over $1.5 trillion in two years flowing into chips, data centers, and power. TSMC is the pinch point and it knows it: Q2 revenue up 36 percent to $40.2 billion, gross margin at 67.7 percent, full-year guidance raised above 40 percent growth, and 5 to 10 percent wafer price hikes going out to Apple, Nvidia, Qualcomm, and AMD. NVIDIA has locked up roughly 60 percent of advanced packaging capacity for 2026 and 2027, so supply, not demand, sets the ceiling. On power, every major hyperscaler has now signed at least one nuclear deal in 2026, nearly a dozen agreements totaling close to 10 gigawatts, with a Washington push on small modular reactors accelerating the timeline. Energy availability is quietly becoming the binding constraint on AI capacity, more than silicon.

#Signal or noise?

Signal. The Microsoft-versus-Meta split is not a one-day earnings quirk, it is the market forcing the AI trade into a show-me-the-revenue phase while a rising long-bond yield raises the cost of financing every gigawatt of that buildout.

#Watch tomorrow

Amazon and Apple report after Thursday's close. Amazon's AWS growth and capex guide will either confirm or break the Microsoft cloud read, and Apple's margin commentary lands against the new TSMC wafer price hikes. Also watch Brent: a sustained hold above $92 turns a geopolitical spike into a genuine airline cost story.

item.title: The Platero Brief, No. 33: Wednesday, July 29, 2026
item.content:encoded:
Executive Pulse

#Macro signal

Fed decides today with a hike, not a cut, on the table: The FOMC announces at 2:00pm ET, with consensus a fifth straight hold at 3.50 to 3.75 percent but markets pricing roughly a 30 percent chance of a rate increase. The June dot plot already flipped the median year-end 2026 rate up to 3.8 percent from 3.4 percent in March, and the IMF's July outlook says global disinflation has stalled, with headline inflation projected to rise to 4.7 percent this year. The direction of surprise is now up, not down. Every AI capex and infrastructure bet is being underwritten at a discount rate that could climb rather than fall, so any 2027 budget defense needs to show payback that survives a hike, not just a hold.

#Tech industry

  • The AI race became a war for electricity, financing, and fiber, and investors started pricing the risk: July 28 brought a cluster of capital moves. Amazon committed roughly 200 billion dollars to AI infrastructure in 2026, Nvidia backed a 50 billion dollar lease for a Texas facility running its own chips, AMD locked up 2.5 gigawatts of capacity from Core Scientific, and Verizon signed a 1 billion dollar dark-fiber deal with Google. At the same time AI chip stocks sold off as the market shifted from "is there demand" to "can trillion-dollar capex clear an adequate return, and when." The bottleneck has moved from models to power, real estate, and the balance sheet, and vendor financing where chipmakers underwrite their own customers' buildouts is circular-demand risk boards should now be probing.
  • The open-weight frontier went Chinese-led: Moonshot AI released Kimi K3, a 2.8-trillion-parameter model under a modified MIT license, giving away frontier-scale capability and undercutting proprietary API economics. Google separately delayed Gemini 3.5 Pro after it missed on coding and reasoning in testing, and Alphabet fell about 4 percent on execution concerns. API-pricing moats are eroding from below while the incumbent leader stumbles on delivery, which makes multi-model architecture a board-level resilience question, not an engineering preference.

#AI at the leadership level

The accountability gap is the story. Roughly 76 percent of organizations now have a Chief AI Officer, up from 26 percent a year ago, but only 14 percent have defined who is accountable for AI results at the C-suite level, and 48 percent of AI projects miss their business objectives, most often because responsibility is undefined between CIO, CDO, and the business units. The org-chart response to AI has outrun the accountability response. The leadership move is not another exec title, it is a written accountability map naming who owns outcomes, plus a continuous-monitoring reporting line to the board, since AI is probabilistic and drifts rather than staying validated once.

#Leadership & org design

McKinsey's State of Organizations 2026, surveying more than 10,000 senior executives across 15 countries, finds 75 percent of organizations are failing to build high-performance cultures, with limited career progression the top barrier at 47 percent, ahead of weak incentives and disengagement. The specific move: the single-leader hierarchy is now treated as the obstacle, with leadership shifting toward teams of leaders holding distributed accountability. The live risk is that AI-driven delayering, visible this week in Visa cutting 2,600 tech and product roles citing automation, kills the very progression paths the data flags as the number-one performance lever. Cut layers without cutting the ladder.

#Question worth asking your team this week

If the board asked tomorrow who personally owns the return on our largest AI investment, and by when it pays back at a discount rate that rises rather than falls, could we name the person and the date?

Practitioner Pulse

#Try this now

  • Record a Skill in Claude Cowork: Screen-record yourself doing a repetitive task once while narrating the steps aloud, and Cowork captures the screen activity, clicks, typing, and voice-over together, then turns it into a structured, rerunnable skill in your library. No prompt writing, no step lists. In the desktop app, use the plus menu, "Record a skill," pick one genuinely repetitive weekly chore (pulling a campaign report, reformatting a brief, QA-ing a UTM sheet), record it once, and rerun it with a click. It removes the automation-authoring bottleneck for non-engineers, the first mainstream teach-by-showing tool, and turns a 30-minute weekly task into a one-click rerun.
  • Route tasks across a multi-model stack: Instead of standardizing on one vendor, send each task to the cheapest model that clears the quality bar, high-value reasoning to a frontier model (Opus 5 shipped July 24 at roughly half the price of Opus 4.8), high-volume grunt work to cheap Flash-tier models. Audit your team's recurring AI tasks, tag each as reasoning-heavy or volume, assign a model tier, and track cost-per-output from day one. Cost efficiency lives in the multi-model stack, not single-vendor lock-in, and only 7 percent of orgs can currently prove AI ROI, so the number matters before your next budget review.
  • Automate AI-answer share-of-voice monitoring: Replace manual spot-checking of how your brand shows up in ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, and Gemini with continuous tracking of citation frequency, sentiment, and competitor share. Stand up a weekly automated query set of your top 20 category questions, log which brands get cited and in what tone, and pair it with an agent-ready catalog audit (clean structured attributes, complete descriptions, machine-readable policies) so shopping agents can actually recommend you. As generative platforms become the first point of contact for buyers, "are we even in the answer" is the new rank-tracking, and it got sharper this week with ChatGPT's self-serve ad platform going live July 27.

#Case study worth stealing

Schnucks, agentic commerce that keeps the data layer in-house: The regional US grocer is embedding an AI shopping assistant directly inside its existing Schnucks Rewards app, powered by VitalityIP's intelligence layer built on billions of lines of shopping, health, and nutrition data mapped to ingredient-level product attributes. The structural detail is the lesson: Schnucks keeps ownership of the customer relationship, shopper data, and brand experience while renting the AI and the database. Any digital team can adapt the tactic, embed the agent inside your own owned surface, the app or loyalty program, rather than handing customers to a third-party assistant, and contractually keep the data and the relationship. For travel and loyalty, swap nutrition guidance for trip planning and points optimization and the pattern is identical.

#Framework or mental model

Context engineering, the four moves: The discipline replacing prompt engineering as the named skill of 2026, now formalized by both the Thoughtworks Technology Radar and LangChain. Where prompt engineering asks what to tell the model, context engineering asks what the model needs to know, using four moves on everything in the context window: Write (persist state outside the prompt), Select (retrieve only relevant data and examples), Compress (summarize to fit the window), and Isolate (split work across separate agents so they do not pollute each other). When an AI workflow gives inconsistent output, the fix is almost always context, not a cleverer prompt, and because all four moves work in a plain chat window with zero code, this is a team-wide literacy play, not an engineering one.

#Rabbit hole

Anthropic's own usage data shows the overwhelming majority of Claude Cowork activity is non-technical knowledge work, scheduling, files, and ops, not software, a useful gut-check on where the real AI-adoption market is versus where the discourse points. VentureBeat's write-up ("most Cowork users aren't coding") is the short version worth reading before your next tooling debate.

AI Stack Daily

#Vendor & platform moves

  • HubSpot: Opened Agent Hub and Agent Builder to all Professional and Enterprise customers. Agent Hub is a single console showing every HubSpot agent by GTM outcome (build demand, win deals, delight customers, scale growth), and Agent Builder is a low-code canvas where non-technical staff assemble agents from their own prompts, knowledge, and CRM data. Custom agents burn metered "HubSpot Credits." Signal: the CRM suites are racing to become the agent orchestration layer, not just the system of record, and the move to consumption pricing is a quiet break from seat-based SaaS economics.
  • Salesforce: Made its Agentforce Commerce Shopper, Buyer, and Merchant agents generally available, with native ChatGPT integration live and Google Search and Gemini following. Signal: Salesforce is planting commerce agents inside third-party AI surfaces rather than only its own UI, because the battleground is moving to where the buyer's agent actually shops. Whoever owns the merchant catalog and checkout wins agentic-commerce distribution, and the agentic CRM race is now the defining suite competition.
  • Google: AI Max exited beta with real numbers, 500,000-plus advertisers and a 15 percent average conversion lift, while Alphabet's Q2 ad revenue grew 14 percent to 81.6 billion dollars. Signal: Google is proving AI-native ad products both convert and monetize at scale, a counterweight to the bearish standalone-chatbot ad narrative, and with model prices collapsing (Opus 5 shipped at half its predecessor's price) the unit economics of embedding agents keep falling.

#Category watch

Agentic advertising: In early July, Meta, Google, Amazon, and OpenAI all shipped agentic ad tooling in the same week, and the framing across trackers is that AI ad tooling crossed from experiment to default. But the revenue thesis is being repriced hard: eMarketer pegs the entire US standalone chatbot ad market at under 1 billion dollars in 2026 and only 5.4 billion by 2030, against OpenAI's reported 100 billion dollar 2030 target. The category is splitting two ways, agentic buying inside the walled gardens is real and monetizing now, while standalone chatbot advertising is being marked down. For a stack builder: invest in agentic execution where inventory and measurement already exist, and treat chatbot ad inventory as experimental, not a budget line.

#Stack intelligence

The composable-CDP value proposition is getting swallowed by the lakehouse. Databricks launched CustomerLake, an agentic CDP embedded directly in the lakehouse, occupying the exact "activate data where it already lives" position that warehouse-native CDP vendors built their pitch on, and Snowflake and BigQuery equivalents are the natural next move. The buy-versus-build line has shifted: the question is no longer "which CDP" but "does my cloud data platform's native agentic CDP make a standalone CDP redundant." For anyone on Databricks, Snowflake, or BigQuery, the default is drifting toward native activation plus a thin best-of-breed layer, and standalone CDP vendors become consolidation targets.

#Foundations concept of the day

Composable CDP: A traditional Customer Data Platform is a standalone system that copies customer data out of your source systems into its own store, then unifies identities and pushes segments to marketing tools. A composable CDP inverts that. Instead of a separate database, it runs unification, identity, and activation directly on top of the cloud data warehouse or lakehouse you already operate, so the data never leaves its system of record. It matters at scale because duplicating billions of customer rows into a separate CDP is expensive, slow, and a governance liability, whereas activating in place keeps one source of truth. A retailer running its transaction history in Snowflake can add identity resolution and audience activation as a layer rather than exporting everything into a second platform, and in 2026 that same layer increasingly ships an agent on top of it.

#Watch list

  • Consumption pricing spreading across CRM suites: HubSpot Credits and Salesforce Agentforce consumption both meter agent usage. If agent cost scales with usage rather than seats, budget planning and vendor-cost forecasting for martech orgs change materially, so watch for cost-predictability tooling and buyer pushback.
  • Retail media's scaled second tier: Amazon and Walmart Connect still take roughly 88 percent of US retail media spend, but DoorDash Ads and Instacart Ads have each crossed about 1 billion dollars in annual US ad revenue. As total US retail media hits 71 billion dollars this year, the next inventory land-grab is in that second tier of delivery and grocery platforms.

Markets Signal

#Macro pulse

Canada: The TSX Composite closed Tuesday at 35,749.70, up 0.51 percent, a fresh record high led by technology. USD/CAD sits near 1.408, roughly flat on the day and range-bound between 1.406 and 1.412 all week, so no international-revenue-translation flag today, though the loonie remains persistently weak in trend terms.

USA (July 28 close): The Dow rallied 1.03 percent to 52,747 on strong earnings and rotation out of semis, the S&P 500 edged up 0.21 percent to a near-record 7,428, and the Nasdaq slipped 0.22 percent, dragged by the chip selloff. The FOMC decision lands today at 2:00pm ET with the presser at 2:30pm, consensus a fifth straight hold at 3.50 to 3.75 percent. Treat the hold as expected, not fact, until the release.

Asia (July 29 session): Seoul's Kospi is the standout, down roughly 6.8 percent intraday as SK Hynix fell about 13 percent (record profit but a forecast miss) and Samsung dropped nearly 8 percent, an AI-capex reality check hitting the chipmakers hardest. The Nikkei fell 1.7 percent, Shanghai slipped 0.5 percent, and Hong Kong's Hang Seng was the lone gainer, up 1.7 percent.

Oil, flag: WTI closed near 81 dollars Tuesday after an 8 percent Monday plunge on US-Iran diplomatic hopes, but reversed hard today as fresh Middle East fighting erupted, with Brent up about 4 percent toward 88 dollars and crude broadly up more than 2 percent. The de-escalation that had cut jet-fuel input costs is unwinding, putting fuel risk back on the table.

#Today's industry move

JetBlue embedded installment flight financing from fintech ClarityPay directly into its TrueBlue loyalty program, with customers earning points on financed bookings. The more strategic Skift thread underneath it: travel customer acquisition is shifting away from Google's open auction toward private bilateral "private treaty" deals that trade loyalty-member access and inventory. For an airline CDO, that is the loyalty data layer becoming the acquisition currency, exactly the asset worth owning rather than renting.

#AI infrastructure watch

The chip stack is the whole story. Tuesday's US session saw AMD fall roughly 10 percent, Broadcom down 4 percent, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index off more than 4 percent, triggered by SK Hynix's miss, signs of progress in China's advanced chipmaking, and optics around NVIDIA reportedly in talks to provide OpenAI a 250 billion dollar backstop to fund a 10-gigawatt Ohio data-center campus. Critics read the backstop as circular vendor financing, NVIDIA underwriting its own largest customer, while for OpenAI it is a first step toward owning infrastructure rather than renting from Microsoft, Amazon, and Oracle. Context: the four hyperscalers are on track for up to 725 billion dollars of mostly-AI capex this year.

#Signal or noise?

Signal. The two-day chip rout is investors repricing AI capex for return timelines rather than doubting demand, and it rhymes with the same ROI scrutiny showing up in the Fed's higher-for-longer stance, a larger trend, not a one-day blip.

#Watch tomorrow

Today's oil reversal is the key watch-item into Air Canada's Q2 results on August 12, and the 2:00pm Fed decision plus any hint of a hike bias could compound the AI-capex repricing already underway.
