item.content:encoded:
Executive Pulse

#Macro signal

Middle East escalation reprices energy and risk: Fresh US strikes on Iranian targets sent WTI crude up more than 4% to roughly $75 on July 13, with equity futures soft and semiconductors leading the slide. For leaders, this is a reminder that the inflation fight is not over on the demand side, it can be reignited from the supply side overnight. May US CPI already ran at 4.2%, its highest since 2023, driven largely by energy. Any 2026 plan built on a smooth disinflation glide path needs an energy-shock branch. The implication for tech, product, and marketing leaders: model a scenario where input costs and consumer discretionary spend move against you at the same time, because an oil spike does both.

#Tech industry

  • Capital rotates from software to AI infrastructure: Adobe, Salesforce, and The Trade Desk all hit 52-week lows this month as investors pulled money out of traditional SaaS and pushed it into AI infrastructure names, even though Adobe posted record revenue of $6.62B up 13%. Strategic implication: the market is pricing a real risk that generative AI erodes the value of premium software subscriptions. Every software-dependent business should have a clear answer to "why does our seat-based pricing survive agents doing the work?"
  • The agent platform war goes to protocols: Google rebranded Vertex AI to the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform and pushed the Agent2Agent protocol into production. Strategic implication: the competitive frontier is moving from model quality to who owns the orchestration and interoperability standard. Betting your stack on a single vendor's agent protocol is a lock-in decision, treat it like one.

#AI at the leadership level

The uncomfortable number this week: roughly 95% of organizations report zero ROI from generative AI investments, and the diagnosed cause is not the technology, it is the operating model. The gap is between deployment and transformation. Notably, line-of-business leaders are now the largest AI decision-making group at 46%, ahead of CIOs and CTOs. AI budget authority is shifting out of central IT and into the functions. Enterprises where senior leadership actively shapes AI governance capture materially more value than those that delegate it to technical teams.

#Leadership & org design

The winning pattern in the 2026 studies is to treat AI as a capability and workflow redesign, not a tool rollout. Organizations scaling AI successfully are redesigning how decisions get made and how authority is distributed, not bolting a copilot onto an unchanged process. The practical move for a leader this quarter: pick one core workflow and redesign it around what agents can now do, rather than spreading a thin layer of AI assistance across everything and getting no ROI anywhere.

#Question worth asking your team this week

If line-of-business owners now hold most of the AI decision rights, what is our operating model for governing dozens of function-led AI initiatives so they compound into one capability instead of fragmenting into forty disconnected pilots?

Practitioner Pulse

#Try this now

  • Hightouch Lifecycle Studio: Runs multi-stage lifecycle campaigns directly off your data warehouse with a visual builder for touchpoints, transactional milestones, and real-time audience logic. No copying data into a separate marketing cloud first. If your customer data already lives in Snowflake, BigQuery, or Databricks, map one onboarding or win-back journey here this week and compare the audience freshness against whatever your ESP is doing on a nightly sync. The activation-from-warehouse pattern is worth the 20 minutes even if you do not switch.
  • ActiveCampaign Google Ads connector for Active Intelligence: New connector pushes your first-party ActiveCampaign segments straight into Google Ads and can spin up Performance Max campaigns from them. The practical win is closing the loop between owned audiences and paid without a manual list export every week. Wire one high-intent segment into a PMax test and watch whether match rates hold.
  • Typeface Ad Agent and Video Agent updates: Ad Agent now auto-resizes a single creative into channel-specific variants, and Video Agent added scene-level editing so you can fix one shot without re-rendering the whole cut. For a lean team shipping paid social across five placements, this collapses the resize-and-version busywork that eats a designer's afternoon.

#Case study worth stealing

ActiveCampaign, closing the owned-to-paid loop from one segment source: Rather than treating email lists and ad audiences as two disconnected systems, the new connector lets a single governed segment drive both lifecycle email and Performance Max spend. The tactic any digital team can copy without buying the tool: pick your best-performing owned segment, define it once in your source of truth, and make that same definition the seed for paid acquisition. The value is not the integration, it is refusing to let "email audience" and "ad audience" drift into two different truths maintained by two different people.

#Framework or mental model

The extraction tax: Every time you copy customer data out of the warehouse into a separate marketing tool, you pay a tax in staleness, duplicated identity logic, and sync lag. The warehouse-native activation movement (Hightouch, Databricks CustomerLake, Snowflake clean rooms) exists because practitioners realized the better move is to keep the data where it lives and plug capabilities in around it. Before your next MarTech purchase, ask what extraction tax it charges and whether the same job could run against the data in place.

AI Stack Daily

#Vendor & platform moves

  • Databricks CustomerLake: Launched as an "agentic CDP" embedded natively in the lakehouse, with Adstra (identity resolution) and Bloomreach as launch partners. Signal: The CDP is migrating down into the data infrastructure layer itself. First the marketing clouds absorbed CDPs (Salesforce Data Cloud, Adobe Real-Time CDP), now the data platforms are absorbing the activation layer from below. The standalone CDP is being squeezed from both directions.
  • Google Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: Google renamed Vertex AI to the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform and folded Agentspace into one product, shipping a no-code agent builder for Workspace, 200-plus models including third-party Claude, and the production Agent2Agent protocol. Signal: The hyperscalers are racing to own the agent orchestration layer, not just the model. Whoever owns the protocol for how agents talk to each other owns the switching costs.
  • ActiveCampaign and Typeface: ActiveCampaign shipped a Google Ads connector that launches Performance Max from owned segments, Typeface added channel-specific ad resizing and scene-level video editing. Signal: The mid-market MarTech tools are converging on the same feature set, owned-audience-to-paid loops plus generative creative variants, which compresses what used to be three vendors into one.

#Category watch

Agentic CDPs: The category is shifting from "unify customer data in a dedicated platform" to "run identity resolution and activation as agents against data that never leaves the warehouse." Databricks CustomerLake, Snowflake clean rooms, and Salesforce Data Cloud are the players. The open question nobody has answered cleanly: autonomous identity resolution at machine speed creates privacy obligations, EU and US state rules on automated decision-making, that most enterprise teams have not mapped. The tech is ahead of the governance.

#Stack intelligence

The warehouse-as-CDP pattern is now the default architecture question, not a fringe one. Enterprises building a new customer stack in 2026 are increasingly deciding to keep the lakehouse as the source of truth and buy thin activation and identity layers around it, rather than buying a monolithic marketing cloud that owns a second copy of the data. The buy-vs-build line has moved: buy the model and the activation connectors, own the data layer.

#Foundations concept of the day

Data clean rooms: A clean room is a secure, neutral environment where two parties match and analyze their data against each other without either side seeing the other's raw records. A retailer and a brand can learn that the same 40,000 people bought both products and measure a campaign's lift, without the retailer handing over its customer list or the brand exposing its buyers. It matters at scale because in a world with fewer third-party cookies, clean rooms are how walled gardens and first-party data owners collaborate legally. Real example: an airline with logged-in loyalty data and a hotel chain can run a clean-room match to size their shared audience and sell a joint media package, with neither exposing individual identities.

#Watch list

  • Adstra: Its identity-resolution role inside CustomerLake is a tell for where independent identity vendors go as CDPs collapse into data platforms. Watch whether more identity specialists become embedded launch partners rather than standalone products.
  • Agent2Agent protocol adoption: If A2A gets traction beyond Google, cross-vendor agent interoperability becomes real and the orchestration layer, not the model, becomes the strategic control point.

Markets Signal

#Macro week in review

Canada: The S&P/TSX composite held up well through the prior week, advancing 0.76% to close near 35,200 on July 9 with broad positive breadth, before slipping about 74 points Monday morning as financials and base metals led a pullback. USD/CAD stayed tied to oil, a rising crude price supports the loonie, which cushions Canadian carrier international costs even as it complicates USD-denominated revenue translation. USA: A choppy week. Semiconductors sold off hard to open the prior week (Nasdaq down 1.16% on July 7, Micron off 4.7%), then chips led a sharp rebound mid-week (Nasdaq up 1.30% July 9). Monday July 13 opened risk-off again: Dow roughly flat, S&P 500 down about 0.3%, Nasdaq down about 0.7% as Asian chip weakness in SK Hynix and Samsung dragged Micron and Sandisk. Asia: Asian chipmakers were the week's pressure point, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics fell hard on the Monday session, exporting weakness into US semiconductor names. Oil / jet fuel: WTI jumped more than 4% to roughly $75 on July 13 after fresh US strikes on Iranian targets, though crude is still down about 7% over the trailing month. A supply-driven spike is the worst kind for airlines, it raises fuel cost without any accompanying demand strength. Rates and data: The June US CPI print lands Tuesday July 14. Consensus looks for a soft headline near 3.9% annual, but that softness is energy base effects, not underlying cooling, and May already ran at 4.2%. Q2 bank earnings (JPMorgan, Goldman, Citi, Wells, BofA Tuesday, Morgan Stanley and BlackRock Wednesday) set the tone. Theme into next week: Supply-side inflation risk from the Gulf is back on the table just as earnings season opens. Travel and consumer discretionary sit directly in the crossfire of higher fuel and squeezed sentiment.

#MarTech & AdTech

  • Adobe, Salesforce, The Trade Desk: All three hit 52-week lows this month as capital rotated out of application-layer software into AI infrastructure. Adobe touched a seven-year low near $218 despite record $6.62B quarterly revenue up 13%. Signal: the market is pricing the risk that agents erode seat-based SaaS value, the application layer is on the defensive.
  • Databricks CustomerLake: Launched as an agentic CDP inside the lakehouse with Adstra and Bloomreach as partners. Signal: activation and identity are migrating into the data platform, squeezing standalone CDP vendors.

#AI models & APIs

  • Google Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: Vertex AI rebranded and consolidated with a no-code agent builder, 200-plus models including Claude, and the production Agent2Agent protocol. Strategic implication: the fight is moving from model quality to owning the agent orchestration and interoperability standard.
  • Anthropic Sonnet 5 and Claude Fable 5: Sonnet 5 shipped at near-Opus performance with introductory $2/$10 per-million pricing, and Claude Fable 5 was redeployed July 1 after an export restriction was lifted. Implication: frontier-adjacent capability keeps getting cheaper, which pressures per-token pricing across the board.
  • OpenAI GPT-5.6: Arrived as three tiers (Sol, Terra, Luna) plus an Ultra mode, with enterprise agent usage via Codex reportedly at three million weekly users. Implication: the majors are segmenting by cost-per-intelligence, not just raw capability.

#Travel & airline tech

  • WestJet Rewards overhaul: WestJet is moving from a currency-based to a points-based system (100 points per prior $1) and, for the first time, letting members reach up to Platinum status without flying, via RBC co-brand card spend. Signal: the direct Canadian competitor is copying the credit-card-driven status model, loyalty status is decoupling from flying.
  • Aeroplan and Club Avolta: Members now earn Aeroplan points across roughly 1,900 Avolta airport retail and F&B outlets. Signal: coalition earn surface is expanding into physical travel retail, more everyday touchpoints feeding the loyalty ledger.

#AI Infrastructure Stack

Raw materials & hardware

  • Water and siting constraints: The Nvidia-Valar nuclear demo centered on a "nearly waterless" 30MW design in Utah. Signal: water and land, not just power, are becoming gating constraints on where compute can physically go.

Chips & semiconductors

  • Semiconductor whipsaw: Chips drove both the prior week's selloff and its rebound, then led Monday's decline again on Asian weakness. Signal: the AI trade is now concentrated enough in a handful of chip names that they set the tape for the whole market.

Cooling & energy

  • Nvidia and Valar Atomics microreactor: On July 1 the two ran a live demo powering Blackwell silicon off Valar's Ward250 microreactor, described as the first small reactor to power a data center. Signal: AI capex is now energy-constrained, not chip-constrained, grid interconnection queues run five to seven years, and microreactors are the workaround.

Data centers & cloud capex

  • The $4 trillion framing: Nvidia's Jensen Huang reiterated that operators may spend up to $4T upgrading infrastructure over five years. Signal: the spend thesis has shifted from GPUs to the full stack of power, cooling, networking, and orchestration.

Stack insight

The through-line this week: the binding constraint on AI has moved down the stack from chips to electrons. Nuclear-adjacent power deals, waterless cooling, and multi-year grid queues now determine what compute comes online in 12 to 18 months. For anyone planning AI-dependent products, capacity and cost are increasingly a function of energy availability, not model releases, and energy is far less elastic than software.

#Funding rounds worth noting

  • Mobile UA agent startup, $7M Series A (led by The Raine Group): Builds user-acquisition agents for mobile game studios. Signal: agentic automation is moving into performance marketing execution, not just content generation.

#M&A signal

Ad tech and MarTech dealmaking cooled in the first half of 2026 (roughly 10 AdTech acquisitions through June versus 36 in all of 2025), with AI the one hot ticket. The recent marquee deals remain Salesforce-Informatica (about $8B) and Adobe-Semrush. The pattern: consolidation is concentrating around data and AI capability, not audience or media supply.

#The week's big bet

The clearest tell this week was capital fleeing application-layer software (Adobe, Salesforce, The Trade Desk at 52-week lows) and piling into AI infrastructure, while Nvidia demonstrated a nuclear-powered data center to solve the energy bottleneck. The market is betting that value in AI accrues to whoever controls compute and the energy to run it, and that seat-priced software sitting on top is exposed. For digital leaders in travel and MarTech, the implication is to treat the data and activation layer you own as the durable asset, and to assume the execution tools riding on top will keep getting cheaper, more agentic, and more commoditized.

Landscape Scan

#The convergence watch (loyalty data → media networks)

The defining pattern held steady this week: carriers continue to build the loyalty-data-into-ad-inventory business, led by United's Kinective Media, which now scales brand reach across the United app and inflight screens and personalizes MileagePlus member offers, with a roster spanning Norwegian Cruise Line, Macy's, Chase, TelevisaUnivision, IHG, and Dentsu. The parallel signal is infrastructure: Databricks CustomerLake launched as an agentic CDP embedded in the lakehouse with Adstra supplying identity resolution. That matters for convergence because the hard part of monetizing loyalty data as media is clean, privacy-safe identity matching at scale, and the tooling to do it inside the data layer is maturing fast. The trend line for any airline without a media network: the gap between United and everyone else widens each quarter this compounds.

#Airline loyalty & digital

  • WestJet Rewards overhaul: The closest Canadian competitor is making its biggest change in 15 years, moving from a currency-based to a points-based system (100 points per prior $1) and, for the first time, allowing members to reach up to Platinum status without flying via RBC World Elite Mastercard spend. Signal: WestJet is explicitly decoupling elite status from flown revenue and tying it to card spend, the same lever Aeroplan relies on, so the Canadian status-competition front is now a co-brand card fight.
  • Air Canada Aeroplan spend-based earning: The shift to earning points on dollars spent rather than distance flown (effective Jan 1, 2026) is now the baseline both major Canadian carriers share. Signal: distance-based earning is dead in Canada, the battleground moves to who has the richer card ecosystem and burn options.

#Hotel & travel loyalty

  • Marriott Bonvoy and United dual-currency offer: A stay-and-fly promotion (July 15 to Sept 30) lets members earn in both currencies across the partnership. Signal: cross-vertical loyalty bundling (hotel plus airline) is a lighter-weight path to the same "own more of the trip" goal that media networks chase.
  • Marriott Bonvoy points devaluation: A quiet 5 to 10% flash devaluation on award pricing plus Series-brand earning changes. Signal: even the top-ranked program is tightening economics, a reminder that dynamic point pricing is a margin lever hotels pull regularly and members increasingly notice.

#MarTech

  • Databricks CustomerLake: Agentic CDP embedded in the lakehouse with Adstra (identity) and Bloomreach as launch partners. Relevance to loyalty stacks: activation and identity resolution are moving into the data platform, which favors a "own the loyalty data layer, rent the activation" architecture over a monolithic marketing cloud.
  • ActiveCampaign and Typeface: New Google Ads/Performance Max connector and generative ad-resizing plus scene-level video editing. Relevance: owned-audience-to-paid loops and generative creative are now table stakes even in mid-market tools, raising the floor on what a lean loyalty marketing team can execute.

#AdTech & retail media

  • Software-to-infrastructure capital rotation: The Trade Desk, Adobe, and Salesforce all hit 52-week lows as investors rotated into AI infrastructure. Relevance to the convergence thesis: independent ad-tech platforms are under pressure, which strengthens the case for first-party data owners (airlines, hotels, retailers) to build media businesses on their own audiences rather than depend on the open programmatic middle.
  • Clean rooms as the convergence plumbing: Snowflake clean rooms and CustomerLake-style matching are the mechanism that lets a loyalty data owner and a brand transact media without exposing raw records. Relevance: this is the enabling layer that makes an airline media network sellable to sophisticated advertisers.

#Loyalty tech vendors

  • Adstra (via Databricks): Its embedded identity-resolution role inside CustomerLake is a build-vs-buy signal, identity is becoming a component you plug into your own data platform rather than a standalone product you route data through. For a carrier weighing loyalty-media infrastructure, the question shifts from "which CDP" to "which identity and activation layers wrap our existing lakehouse."

#Strategic implication

The two forces to watch converged this week: United keeps extending its media-network lead while the identity-and-activation plumbing (agentic CDPs in the lakehouse, clean-room matching) matures enough for followers to move. The single most important question for a carrier without a media network is no longer "should we build one" but "can we assemble the first-party data, identity, and clean-room layers fast enough before the category standard is set by United." Meanwhile the Canadian loyalty fight has narrowed to co-brand card economics as both Air Canada and WestJet decouple status from flying. Own the loyalty data layer, buy the identity and activation components around it, and treat a media network as the monetization endpoint of that data asset, not a separate initiative.

item.content:encoded:
Executive Pulse

#Macro signal

Oil back as a strategic variable: WTI rose roughly 4% on the week on fresh US-Iran strikes and a broken ceasefire, settling near $71 after a mid-week spike. For any leader with fuel, logistics, or discretionary-demand exposure, the signal is that geopolitical supply risk is repricing faster than the macro data. With CPI and PPI landing this week and Treasury yields above 4.5%, the strategic posture is to stress-test plans against an energy shock and a higher-for-longer rate path at the same time, rather than assuming either resolves cleanly.

#Tech industry

  • Microsoft stands up a 6,000-person AI consulting arm: Microsoft launched Microsoft Frontier Company, a $2.5B initiative deploying 6,000 industry experts to help enterprises plan and deploy AI. Strategic implication: the frontier labs and hyperscalers have concluded that the bottleneck to AI revenue is not model capability, it is enterprise adoption. When your platform vendor starts selling you the change management, read it as an admission that the technology is ready and the organizations are not.
  • Enterprise becomes the AI revenue engine: Enterprise now exceeds 40% of OpenAI revenue and is tracking toward parity with consumer by year end. Implication: the center of gravity in AI is shifting from consumer novelty to enterprise deployment, which rewards vendors with security, governance, and integration over those with the flashiest demo.

#AI at the leadership level

The adoption data is a leadership indictment, not a technology story. 79% of organizations report challenges adopting AI, up double digits year over year, and 54% of C-suite executives say AI adoption is tearing their company apart. The root cause is structural: 48% introduced AI without redesigning the workflows or roles it sits in, and only 12% have redesigned at scale with a new operating model. AI dropped onto an unchanged org chart produces friction, not leverage. The differentiated companies are treating adoption as operating-model redesign, not a tools rollout.

#Leadership & org design

The 12% who redesigned their operating model around AI are the control group worth studying. The pattern is not "add AI to every role," it is redrawing where decisions are made, which steps get automated, and which keep a human in the loop, then rebuilding roles around that. Spending over $1M a year on AI while leaving the workflow untouched, which many are doing, is how you get high investment and low return in the same quarter.

#Question worth asking your team this week

Where have we bolted AI onto an unchanged process, and what would this function look like if we redesigned the workflow around the AI instead of the reverse?

Practitioner Pulse

#Try this now

  • Context engineering over prompt engineering: The field has quietly moved past clever wording. Treat the model's input as a managed system, not a sentence. Four moves to run this week on any agent or GPT you own: write (persist context outside the window so it survives a reset), select (retrieve only what the current step needs), compress (summarize running history to save tokens), isolate (give each sub-task its own clean context). The counterintuitive rule: models take 1M-token windows, but answer quality degrades past roughly 50K tokens of genuinely relevant context. Stuffing the window is now an anti-pattern. Audit one production prompt and cut everything that is not load-bearing.
  • Measure agents like a P&L, not a demo: The teams pulling ahead track tokens per successful task, context-window utilization, retrieval precision and recall, and cost per task against a fixed evaluation set. If you run any AI workflow, stand up a 20-case eval set this week and start logging success rate and cost per run. You cannot improve what you are not scoring, and "it feels better" is not a metric a CFO accepts.
  • Treat prompts as company assets: The smartest operators are versioning prompts, scoping them to narrow well-defined jobs, keeping human review on anything customer-facing, and storing the winners as reusable IP. The advantage is shifting from who has the best model to who structures decisions, approvals, and feedback loops best.

#Case study worth stealing

CVS Media Exchange, closed-loop measurement on loyalty data: CVS launched CorIQ, an AI-driven measurement platform built directly on ExtraCare loyalty data, tying ad exposure to actual in-store and online purchase. The move any digital team can adapt: the asset is not the ad inventory, it is the identity spine that connects a logged-in customer across exposure and conversion. If you hold a loyalty or account relationship, you already own the one thing advertisers and internal stakeholders will pay for, closed-loop proof that spend moved behavior. Build the measurement layer on your first-party identity before you build more media.

#Framework or mental model

Write, Select, Compress, Isolate: The four primitives of context engineering for any AI agent. Write persists state beyond the current window. Select pulls in only what this step needs. Compress summarizes to protect the token budget. Isolate hands sub-tasks their own uncluttered context so one messy step does not poison the whole run. Digital leaders can apply the same discipline to human workflows: most bad decisions come from the same failure modes, no memory, too much irrelevant input, no summarization, and no separation of concerns.

AI Stack Daily

#Vendor & platform moves

  • Agency holdcos are buying the data layer: WPP acquired data clean room vendor InfoSum, folding it into its WPP Open operating system, while Publicis grabbed identity and data company Lotame to bolt onto Epsilon's 2.3 billion profiles. Signal: the agencies have stopped renting first-party data infrastructure and started owning it. When the middlemen vertically integrate into identity and clean rooms, the message to every enterprise is that the data collaboration layer, not the creative layer, is where durable margin now sits. InfoSum also hands WPP a large, diverse dataset for training AI, so the clean room doubles as a model-training moat.
  • CVS Media Exchange ships CorIQ: A retailer stood up an AI-driven closed-loop measurement platform on its own loyalty data. Signal: retail media is maturing from selling impressions to selling proof. The networks that win the next 18 months are the ones that can attribute exposure to purchase on first-party identity, which pressures every non-retailer with a logged-in audience to ask why they are not doing the same.

#Category watch

Data clean rooms and CDPs converging: The old framing of CDP versus clean room is collapsing into "you need both." The CDP resolves and activates your own first-party data; the clean room lets you match it against a partner's without either side exposing raw records. With cookie deprecation and privacy law forcing the issue, the enterprise stack is reorganizing around a resolution-and-collaboration core, and vendors that only do one half are the acquisition targets, not the acquirers.

#Stack intelligence

MarTech M&A ran 37 to 47 deals per quarter through 2025 with over $25 billion in tracked deal value, and two catalysts drive nearly all of it: acquiring AI-native capability, and acquiring first-party data infrastructure (CDPs, identity resolution, consent management) ahead of cookie loss. The practical read for anyone building a stack: the buy-versus-build line has moved. Identity and collaboration are being bought because they are too slow to build against a regulatory clock, while activation and orchestration are increasingly built in-house on top.

#Foundations concept of the day

Data clean room: A secure, neutral environment where two parties match and analyze their data against each other without either seeing the other's raw records. Party A uploads its customer list, Party B uploads its own, the room returns only aggregated overlap and insights, never row-level data. It matters at scale because it is how a brand and a publisher (or two retailers) collaborate on audiences in a cookieless, privacy-regulated world. Example: a consumer packaged goods brand and a grocery chain use a clean room to find shared shoppers and measure whether the brand's ads drove in-store sales, without the grocer handing over its loyalty file or the brand exposing its CRM.

#Watch list

  • TSMC Q2 earnings, July 16: guidance on CoWoS advanced-packaging capacity and any capex revision is the clearest read on whether the AI infrastructure buildout is still accelerating or hitting a ceiling.
  • Retail media measurement standardization: as more networks ship closed-loop tools on loyalty data, watch for the first credible cross-retailer measurement standard. Whoever sets it controls the category's currency.

Markets Signal

#Macro pulse

Weekend, markets closed. The read carries from Friday's close. Canada: the S&P/TSX Composite gained 0.3% to 35,305, near a record high after a stronger-than-expected jobs report, with financials mixed as a firm economy eased pressure on the Bank of Canada to cut. USA: the S&P 500 rose 0.4% to finish near its highs ahead of this week's June CPI and PPI prints, with Treasury yields holding above 4.5% and the Fed leaning hawkish. Oil: WTI settled at $71.41 Friday, down under 1% on the day but up about 4% on the week on fresh US-Iran strikes and a broken ceasefire, the kind of geopolitical supply move that hits airline margins directly.

#AI infrastructure watch

TSMC reports Q2 earnings July 16, the week's single most important infrastructure read. Watch three things: CoWoS advanced-packaging capacity (the current chokepoint in the AI chip supply chain), full-year revenue guidance, and any revision to the $52B to $56B 2026 capex budget, already the largest in the company's history at roughly 37% above 2025. Whether that number moves up or holds is the clearest available signal on whether the AI buildout is still accelerating.

#Signal or noise?

The oil move is signal, not noise: renewed US-Iran conflict reintroduces a supply-risk premium that had faded, and it lands the same week as inflation data, so energy and rates are set to move demand-sensitive sectors together.

#Watch tomorrow

US June CPI and PPI this week, and the start of earnings season with the big banks Tuesday. Both set the tone for whether the near-record equity levels hold.

Executive Pulse

#Macro signal

AI spend is doubling, and CEOs now own the decision: Corporations expect to roughly double AI spending in 2026, from about 0.8% to 1.7% of revenues, and nearly three quarters of CEOs now say they are their organization's primary decision maker on AI, twice last year's share. Why it matters strategically: AI has crossed from an IT line item to a CEO-owned bet, which means the accountability for return sits at the top and the tolerance for vague pilots is falling. The implication for tech, product, and marketing leaders: expect to defend AI investment in ROI terms to a CEO who now considers it their call, not yours.

#Tech industry

  • OpenAI ships GPT 5.6 and ChatGPT Work: A new tiered model family paired with an integrated AI workspace unifying chat, coding, and productivity. Strategic implication: the assistant is becoming the operating surface for knowledge work, which pressures every SaaS vendor whose value was a dedicated interface a worker no longer needs to open.
  • Accenture and Google Cloud target the mid-market: A suite of pre-built agentic solutions aimed at companies with $300M to $3B revenue. Strategic implication: agentic AI is being packaged for firms without the engineering bench to build it, compressing the capability gap between enterprises and their smaller, faster competitors.

#AI at the leadership level

The constraint on AI has moved from model capability to organizational readiness. Adoption is now bottlenecked by organizational design, fragmented data, and a shortage of implementation talent, not by whether the model is smart enough. Agency and vendor AI capability is outrunning clients' ability to approve, fund, govern, and measure it. The CDO mandate is shifting accordingly: the job is no longer sourcing technology, it is building the governance, data architecture, and operating model to deploy it responsibly at scale. The organizations that win the next 18 months will be the ones that fixed their data and decision rights, not the ones that picked the best model.

#Leadership & org design

The pattern in this week's CEO research is a widening execution gap: near-universal belief that AI agents will produce measurable returns in 2026, paired with candid admission that most organizations cannot yet approve, fund, and govern deployments fast enough to capture them. The practical read for a leadership team is that the binding constraint is internal velocity, not external technology. The highest-leverage move right now is redesigning the approval, funding, and measurement path for AI work so it moves at the speed of the capability, rather than adding more pilots to a queue no one can clear.

#Question worth asking your team this week

If our AI capability is now ahead of our ability to approve, fund, and measure it, what is the single approval or governance bottleneck we could remove this quarter that would unlock the most stalled value?

Sources: BCG AI Radar 2026: CEOs take the lead, AI news week of July 10, AI Update July 10 2026

Practitioner Pulse

#Try this now

  • Claude Sonnet 5 for agent workflows: Anthropic's new midsize model plans, uses tools (browser, terminal), and completes multi-step work at a fraction of frontier-model cost. If you have an internal automation stalled because the "smart enough" model was too expensive to run at volume, re-price it against Sonnet 5 this week. The economics of agentic workflows just shifted, and most teams are still budgeting against last quarter's rate card.
  • Nano Banana 2 Lite for creative production: Google's fast, low-cost image model (available to developers June 30) is built for the exact grind marketing teams hate, ad variants, product visuals, social creative at volume. Point it at your next campaign's creative brief and generate 20 variants before you brief an agency. Use it to widen the funnel of ideas, not to replace the final asset.
  • ChatGPT Work + GPT 5.6: OpenAI's integrated workspace unifies chat, coding, and productivity in one surface with the new tiered model. Worth 20 minutes to see whether it collapses the tool-switching tax your team pays jumping between a chat window, a doc, and a code sandbox.

#Case study worth stealing

Salesforce commerce customers, exposing catalogs to agent surfaces: Salesforce made its Shopper, Buyer, and Merchant agents generally available July 6, with native integration into ChatGPT and Google Search AI Mode coming. The number that matters: retailers running their own shopper agents grew sales 59% faster than those on the sidelines. The adaptable tactic is not "buy Agentforce." It is that your product and pricing data now needs to be legible to autonomous agents, not just to human browsers. Any digital org should be asking whether its catalog, inventory, and commerce APIs are agent-readable this quarter, because the shopping surface is moving from your site to someone else's assistant.

#Framework or mental model

Context engineering (write, select, compress, isolate): As agents run longer and accumulate history, the context window fills with noise and decisions degrade, a failure mode now called context rot. The discipline that replaces prompt-tweaking has four moves: write (persist context outside the window), select (retrieve only what is relevant now), compress (summarize to save tokens), isolate (give sub-tasks their own clean context). A 2026 survey found 82% of data leaders say prompt engineering alone is no longer sufficient for production. Where digital leaders apply it: any agent you deploy internally will live or die on what information it sees at each step, so treat context design as an architecture decision, not a copywriting one.

Sources: Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 and Google image models, Salesforce Agentforce Commerce GA, Context engineering guide

AI Stack Daily

#Vendor & platform moves

  • Salesforce Agentforce Commerce: Shopper, Buyer, and Merchant agents went generally available July 6, with native placement inside ChatGPT and Google Search AI Mode on the roadmap. Signal: the commerce vendors are racing to make themselves the plumbing behind third-party agent surfaces, not the destination. The buy interface is decoupling from the brand's own site, and the platform that owns the agent-to-catalog connection captures the transaction.
  • HubSpot Revenue Hub: Commerce Hub was renamed Revenue Hub with quoting, tax, financing, and payments folded in, while Breeze AI spread into global search, email composition, mobile meeting prep, and a Microsoft 365 Copilot integration. Signal: the mid-market suites are consolidating point features into fewer, agent-fronted hubs. Every standalone tool doing one of those jobs just lost shelf space inside the suite.

#Category watch

Agentic commerce infrastructure: The category forming fastest right now sits between the CRM/commerce suites and the consumer AI assistants. Salesforce, and by parallel strategy Adobe and HubSpot, are all repositioning as infrastructure for AI agents rather than interfaces for humans. The players to watch are whoever controls the agent surface (OpenAI, Google) and whoever controls the structured commerce data (the suites). The open question for anyone building a stack: when the shopper is an agent, does your martech investment make your data more agent-legible, or just prettier for a human who is no longer the one clicking?

#Stack intelligence

The consolidation pattern this week is suites absorbing adjacent point solutions under an agent layer, HubSpot pulling payments and tax into Revenue Hub, Salesforce fronting commerce with three agents. For anyone running a stack, the buy-vs-build calculus is shifting: the value is no longer in the feature, which the suite will absorb, but in the proprietary first-party data and the orchestration logic that sits above any single vendor. Own the data layer and the decisioning, rent the execution surfaces, because the execution surfaces are the part being commoditized into agents this year.

#Foundations concept of the day

Clean rooms: A data clean room is a secure, privacy-safe environment where two parties (say a retailer and a brand, or an airline and an advertiser) match and analyze their data without either side seeing the other's raw records. Only aggregated, anonymized results come out. It works by matching on hashed identifiers inside a neutral space, so a brand can learn "your loyalty members who saw my ad bought 20% more" without ever receiving a customer list. Why it matters at scale: as third-party cookies disappear, clean rooms are how first-party data gets activated across partners without violating privacy law. Real example: only 48% of US retail media networks currently offer clean room capability, which makes it a live differentiator, not table stakes, for any data owner building an ad business.

#Watch list

  • Agent-readable catalogs: the quiet infrastructure race is making product, inventory, and pricing data consumable by autonomous agents. Watch which vendors ship agent-facing commerce APIs, because that plumbing decides who captures agent-driven sales.

Sources: Salesforce Agentforce Commerce GA, HubSpot July 2026 updates, First-party data and clean rooms in retail media

Markets Signal

#Macro pulse

Markets are closed for the weekend, so this is the read off Friday's close. The tape ended the week firmly risk-on, led by a rebound in the AI trade and softer oil.

  • Canada: The S&P/TSX Composite gained roughly 0.3% Friday to close near 35,305, adding to a solid week. Falling crude is a mixed signal for the index given its energy weighting, but the broad move was up.
  • USA: The S&P 500 closed Thursday at 7,543.64 (+0.8%) and pushed higher again Friday toward 7,575. The Nasdaq led, closing Thursday at 26,206.89 (+1.3%) on renewed AI momentum, with the Dow up to roughly 52,637. Breadth favored semiconductors and AI names.
  • Oil: WTI (August) slipped about 67 cents to near US$71.41 and Brent eased 0.4% to US$76.01, despite the ongoing Middle East conflict. For a Canadian carrier, softer crude is a tailwind on fuel cost even as it pressures the petro side of USD/CAD.

#AI infrastructure watch

The signal of the week sits below the application layer. Nvidia and startup Valar Atomics ran Blackwell AI chips off the Ward250 microreactor in Utah on July 1, the first small modular reactor to power a data center, and are weighing a 30-megawatt, nearly waterless facility using Nvidia's water-efficient cooling. This is the concrete expression of the theme that AI capex is now energy-constrained and the industry is going behind the meter to escape grid limits, following the Microsoft-Constellation and Amazon-Susquehanna nuclear pattern.

#Signal or noise?

Signal. The equity move is one week of momentum, but the energy-for-compute buildout is a multi-year structural constraint, and behind-the-meter nuclear is the clearest tell yet on what will gate AI capacity in 12 to 18 months.

Whether the AI-led rally has legs into next week's US CPI print, and whether crude keeps sliding despite the Middle East war, since both feed directly into airline cost and consumer discretionary demand.

Executive Pulse

#Macro signal

Higher-for-longer is now the base case, not the risk case: With the funds rate held at 3.50-3.75% and 2026 inflation revised up to 3.6%, futures now price the path drifting toward 4% by year-end under a more hawkish Fed. The strategic read: the era of assuming rate relief is bailing out weak unit economics is over. Growth plans that only pencil out with cheaper capital next year need to pencil out at today's cost of money. For tech and product leaders, that means ruthless prioritization of the roadmap toward things that generate cash inside 12 months, not 36. Discount-rate discipline is back as a board conversation.

#Tech industry

  • AI infrastructure demand is real and it is bifurcating the market: Micron posted fiscal Q3 revenue of $41.5B (up from $9.3B a year prior) on DRAM and NAND tied to AI buildout, and semis led the tape higher. The strategic implication is a widening gap between companies selling AI capacity and companies still trying to prove AI ROI. If you are a buyer, supplier pricing power is rising. Lock capacity and terms now rather than assuming the AI cost curve bends in your favor next quarter.
  • Palantir's 84.7% revenue growth signals where budget is actually landing: The money is moving to platforms that operationalize AI against proprietary data, not standalone models. The lesson for any org: differentiation is your data plus your workflows, not access to a frontier model everyone else can also rent.

#AI at the leadership level

The governance gap is now a board liability, and the regulatory clock is doing something unusual: moving. Fresh data shows 55% of enterprises actively deploying AI but only 26% with governance frameworks that keep pace, and 60% of executives expect their board to intervene over a botched AI strategy. Meanwhile the EU AI Act's high-risk obligations, long fixed to August 2, 2026, are now slated for deferral under the Digital Omnibus (stand-alone high-risk systems pushed toward December 2027), pending formal publication before the August date. Do not read the delay as a reprieve. The transparency obligations and enforcement architecture still land, and 78% of organizations have taken no meaningful compliance steps. The board move: treat AI governance as a standing committee item with a named owner, not a legal cleanup you can time to a deadline that keeps shifting.

#Leadership & org design

The flattening is producing measurable results when paired with real enablement, not just headcount math. Average span of control has climbed from roughly 8 in 2013 to 12+ today and is trending toward 25 by 2028. The instructive case: one large industrial reported customer teams doubling revenue in a single 90-day cycle and a product reaching market a year early after cutting management layers from 11-12 down to 6-7. The nuance that separates winners from cargo-cult flatteners: wider spans only work when you invest in the conditions (clear decision rights, better tooling, AI-assisted coordination) that let a manager actually lead 14 people. Removing the layer without funding the enablement just moves the bottleneck up.

#Question worth asking your team this week

If our cost of capital stays near 4% and never comes down, which two things on our roadmap do we kill this quarter, and which one do we double down on because it pays back inside a year?

Practitioner Pulse

#Try this now

  • Corvic AI V5 (prompt-to-workflow): Turns a plain-language prompt into a repeatable, versioned workflow instead of a one-off answer. Take one ad-hoc request your team keeps re-doing by hand (weekly campaign QA, a recurring competitive scan, a data pull) and describe it once. You get a standardized process you can rerun and hand off. Worth 20 minutes because it converts tribal knowledge into a durable asset, not another throwaway chat.
  • Wrike Conversational AI Agent Builder: Build custom task automations in Wrike by describing them in natural language, no scripting. If your team already lives in Wrike, spend 20 minutes automating one intake-to-assignment path (brief submitted, fields validated, owner assigned, due date set). It removes the manual triage tax on every new request.
  • Akeneo Agentic Ziggy (shipped July 8): An agent layer over the product catalog that runs continuous completeness checks across millions of SKUs and auto-simplifies retailer syndication errors into plain guidance. For any commerce or content team, point a data-quality agent at your worst catalog and let it flag the gaps that suppress discovery. The practical hook: as AI-driven discovery replaces browse and search, product data quality is now a ranking input, not back-office hygiene.

#Case study worth stealing

Salesforce, Agentforce Commerce GA (July 6): Salesforce shipped three specialized agents, Shopper (discovery to checkout to service), Buyer (B2B inside WhatsApp and SMS), and Merchant (catalog and merchandising in plain language), and reports early customers seeing double-digit lifts in both conversion and add-to-cart. The load-bearing stat for any digital team: AI-referred traffic converts at roughly eight times the rate of social, and retailers running their own shopper agents grew sales 59% faster than those sitting it out. You do not need Salesforce to steal the move. Split the shopping journey into narrow agent roles rather than one do-everything bot, and instrument AI-referral as its own high-intent traffic source so it stops getting buried in your generic organic bucket.

#Framework or mental model

MAP (Model, Assumptions, Plan): Before executing, write down your model of how the thing works, the assumptions that model depends on, and only then the plan. It forces the hidden assumptions into the open where they can be tested cheaply, which is exactly where most product and marketing bets quietly fail. Use it on your next roadmap or campaign call: spend the first ten minutes listing assumptions and the riskiest one becomes the thing you validate this sprint instead of six weeks in.

AI Stack Daily

#Vendor & platform moves

  • Omneky: Shipped a public API and an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server today, exposing its autonomous ad-creative engine to any AI agent. Pass a single brand URL and it reads positioning, colors, and fonts, writes headline and CTA, and renders on-brand ads in every aspect ratio. Signal: Creative generation is becoming a callable service inside agent workflows, not a seat in a tool. The unit of adtech is shifting from a UI a marketer logs into to an endpoint an agent invokes. Plan your stack around who owns the orchestration layer that calls these endpoints.
  • BlueConic / Blueshift: BlueConic (capture and unify first-party behavioral data) acquired Blueshift (cross-channel decision-and-execute engine for email, SMS, push, in-app, web). Combined base is 600-plus customers across CPG, retail, DTC, and travel. Signal: The CDP category is collapsing the wall between the data layer and the activation layer. A CDP that only unifies profiles is now a feature, not a product. Buyers should re-scope RFPs around closed-loop decisioning, not schema unification.
  • Databricks / CustomerLake: Databricks' agentic CDP, launched mid-June, runs Customer 360, identity resolution, audience building, and activation natively on the lakehouse with no separate CDP data store, governed by Unity Catalog. Private preview names HP, Circle K, and AB InBev. Signal: The data-warehouse vendors are attacking the standalone CDP from below. If the customer data already lives in the lakehouse, the composable-CDP thesis (rent activation, own the data layer) gets a native home and the packaged CDP loses its reason to hold a copy of your data.

#Category watch

Agentic CDP: The customer-data layer is being redrawn in a single quarter. Databricks CustomerLake, BlueConic-Blueshift, and warehouse-native players are all converging on the same claim: unify the data, then let agents decide and act on it continuously rather than in scheduled campaigns. For anyone building a martech org, the practical shift is that "CDP" now spans two jobs that used to be separate purchases (data unification and real-time decisioning), and the incumbents that only do the first are acquisition targets or feature-fodder. Evaluate on where the decisioning loop lives and whether it can run without exporting your data to a vendor's black box.

#Stack intelligence

Enterprises are increasingly building the customer-data layer where the data already sits (the lakehouse or warehouse) and treating activation, messaging, and creative as swappable services called on top of it. The tell is the MCP server: Omneky, Mirakl Ads, and Dynamics 365 Commerce all shipped MCP-native surfaces this cycle, which means the stack is being wired for agent-to-agent invocation, not human-to-UI. The org implication is that your leverage moves upstream to owning the profile store, the identity spine, and the governance layer, while execution tools become interchangeable behind an orchestration agent. Design for portability at the activation edge and defensibility at the data core.

#Foundations concept of the day

Retail media networks (RMNs): A retail media network is an advertising business a retailer builds on top of its own store, app, and first-party purchase data. Instead of only selling products, the retailer sells ad placements (sponsored listings on-site, off-site programmatic, in-store screens) to the brands that want to reach its shoppers, and it targets and measures those ads using its own transaction data. It matters at scale because it is one of the few high-margin, first-party-data-native ad channels left standing as third-party cookies decay: the retailer already knows who bought what, so attribution is closed-loop and does not depend on external tracking. Cross-industry, this is no longer just Amazon and Walmart. Grocery, specialty retail, and food-delivery players are standing up networks (LiveRamp is piloting agentic tooling specifically for grocery and delivery commerce media), and the same logic extends to any business with a logged-in audience and transaction history: a bank, an airline, or a travel platform can run the identical playbook by monetizing its own audience for partner brands. The strategic question for a leader is not whether to buy RMN inventory but whether your own first-party data qualifies you to build one.

#Watch list

  • MCP as the adtech integration standard: A finalized MCP spec is expected July 28. If it lands, expect a wave of "MCP-native" ad servers and creative engines through Q3, and integration strategy stops being about API connectors and starts being about which agent orchestrates the calls. Watch who publishes servers first, because early standard-setters shape the category.
  • Fox / Roku: Fox's $22B agreement for Roku (100M-plus streaming households, first-party CTV data, expected close first half 2027) consolidates content, a connected-TV platform, and a data spine under one owner. Watch for the identity and clean-room implications: another walled garden of logged-in TV viewership tightening around a single ad stack.

Markets Signal

#Macro pulse

Canada: USD/CAD sits near 1.416, off its recent lows and inside the tight 1.41 to 1.42 range, so no signal for international revenue math today. The loonie's slow grind stronger remains the medium-term story, not a Friday event. USA: quiet open with the indices split. Dow +0.2% to ~52,535, S&P 500 +0.2% to ~7,559, Nasdaq +0.1% to ~26,234, Russell 2000 down 0.5%. Bond yields stay stubbornly high and consumer borrowing is softening, the two things keeping the melt-up honest. VIX at 15.7, calm. Asia: mixed. Shanghai Composite pushed above 4,037 (+1.7% on the session prior), Hang Seng firm near 24,175, Nikkei elevated around 70k. WTI is the real mover: down 2.3% to ~$71.80 after a surprise ~3M barrel US crude build, the first weekly stockpile gain since April. Brent above $76 on Strait of Hormuz friction.

#Today's industry move

SK Hynix debuts on Nasdaq under SKHYV (converts to SKHY July 13), pricing 177.9M ADSs at $149 to raise ~$26.5B. Largest ADR offering in market history, bigger than Alibaba's 2014 listing. This is the memory maker behind the HBM stacked next to nearly every AI accelerator at Microsoft, Amazon, Google, and Meta. A foreign chipmaker choosing US markets to fund fabs is a direct read on where the AI capital is priced. Separately, Delta beat with $1.56 EPS vs $1.48 expected on $17.67B revenue, and guided Q3 to $2.00 to $2.50 with mid-teens revenue growth. Bastian's tell for the whole travel sector: fares stay strong on disciplined capacity, and the industry now passes fuel costs through to consumers rather than eating margin. DAL still fell ~2.4% on the fuel line, but the pricing-power thesis is the durable signal for any premium carrier.

#AI infrastructure watch

The SK Hynix listing is the infrastructure story today. HBM is the physical bottleneck on AI capacity, and a $26.5B raise earmarked for new fabs and equipment tells you the memory shortage is real enough to fund at scale. Korea-listed Hynix is up ~770% over twelve months, outrunning Micron's ~700%. Chip stocks softened into the debut on nerves about whether this marks a top. The quieter structural shift underneath: Broadcom's custom ASICs for Alphabet and Meta are eating NVIDIA's narrative, with custom silicon forecast to compound faster than merchant accelerators. NVIDIA is up only ~3% YTD while AMD has ripped past 170%. The accelerator monopoly is fragmenting toward custom.

#Signal or noise?

Signal on infrastructure, blip on the tape: the SK Hynix mega-listing and the ASic-versus-GPU divergence are structural repricings of the AI stack, while today's flat indices and the oil dip are noise.

#Watch tomorrow

Where SKHYV settles after its first full session. A strong close narrows the "Korea discount" and validates the AI trade; a fade would be the first crack in the memory-shortage narrative.

Executive Pulse

#Macro signal

US-Iran conflict escalates into a second day, but markets are compartmentalizing: The US struck ~90 Iranian targets and Iran retaliated against US-allied Middle East countries, putting a fragile truce to the test. Oil rose again (WTI ~$74.49, Brent ~$79.10) yet equities steadied and even rose on the AI trade (Nasdaq +0.6%). Why it matters strategically: the market is treating this as a contained energy-supply risk, not a systemic one, so far. The leadership read is to hold two scenarios at once, plan for a sustained fuel-cost step-up while not overreacting into demand-destruction assumptions the tape isn't yet pricing. The decision this creates: which cost hedges do you put on now while it's still cheap to be early, versus wait.

#Tech industry

  • AI trade shrugs off war jitters; SK Hynix debut looms: Investors rotated back into AI names ahead of SK Hynix's Friday Nasdaq listing (~7x oversubscribed on HBM demand). Strategic implication: capital is still crowding into the AI-infrastructure layer even amid geopolitical shock, a signal that boards see compute/memory supply as the durable scarce asset regardless of the news cycle.
  • Assistant platforms move on commerce: OpenAI's global full-duplex voice rollout and Meta/Google embedding generative creative into ad platforms mean the interface between brands and customers is consolidating into a few AI front-ends. Strategic implication: distribution risk. Leaders should ask whether their brand is reachable and transactable inside these assistants, or is becoming something they merely summarize.

#AI at the leadership level

The center of gravity for AI decisions has moved firmly to the CEO, but governance hasn't caught up. Roughly three-quarters of CEOs now call themselves the chief AI decision-maker (2x last year) and firms plan to nearly double AI spend, yet only ~38% of large companies have a Chief AI Officer with no agreement on reporting lines, and a majority of C-suite leaders describe adoption as organizationally straining. The pattern for org-builders: authority is centralizing at the top faster than the operating model, accountability structures, and change management beneath it can absorb, which is precisely why most GenAI programs still show thin ROI.

#Leadership & org design

The winning digital-leadership mandate is being redefined around adoption, not tooling. The recurring 2026 move of retitling the CIO as CDO is explicitly about the human connection to technology, getting the organization to use AI well, rather than selecting or standing up the tech. The durable insight: in a year when everyone has access to the same models, competitive advantage accrues to the org that changes its behavior fastest, which is a leadership and change-management problem, not a procurement one.

#Question worth asking your team this week

As AI assistants become the front-end for search, service, and commerce, where is our brand currently reachable as an agent-callable action versus merely described, and what would it take to be transactable inside the assistants our customers actually use?

Practitioner Pulse

#Try this now

  • Meta's new reasoning image generator: Rolling out across Facebook, Messenger, and Advantage+, it adds advanced reasoning, in-place photo editing, room/scene redesign, and reliable text rendering (the old failure mode). The 20-minute win for a marketing team: test it for ad-creative variation and localized scene swaps before commissioning shoots. The catch worth flagging to legal now, not later: public Instagram images may feed both the generation and Meta's AI training, so pressure-test consent and rights before you put customer or UGC imagery through it.
  • OpenAI full-duplex voice (GPT-5.5): The new voice model listens and speaks simultaneously (real turn-taking, not walkie-talkie), with GPT-5.5 reasoning and live web search, rolling out globally in ChatGPT. Actionable use: prototype a voice concierge or interruption-tolerant support flow this week. Full-duplex is the difference between a demo and something a customer will actually tolerate on the phone.
  • Google Marketing Live tools (measurement + creative): New Search, YouTube, Shopping, creative-production and measurement betas surfaced at GML. The practical move: get someone on your team into the measurement betas now, because incrementality and creative-at-scale features are where the near-term budget efficiency is, not the flashy generation demos.

#Case study worth stealing

SK Hynix, demand as strategy signal: SK Hynix's US listing priced into ~7x oversubscription ahead of a Friday Nasdaq debut, driven entirely by AI-memory (HBM) demand. The steal isn't financial, it's a planning lesson: the constraint on what your AI roadmap can ship in 12-18 months is increasingly memory and compute supply, not model quality. Digital teams should treat "can we actually get the capacity" as a first-class question in AI planning, the same way they'd treat headcount.

#Framework or mental model

Full-duplex vs half-duplex interaction: Borrowed from telecom. Half-duplex means one party transmits at a time (early voice assistants: you talk, it waits, it talks). Full-duplex means both directions are live at once, so either side can interrupt. As AI interfaces go full-duplex, the design problem shifts from scripting turns to managing interruption, overlap, and repair. Any team building conversational product should start designing for barge-in and correction now, because users will expect it the moment they've used one good full-duplex agent.

Sources: Stock Market Today July 9, TheStreet, Latest AI-powered martech news, MarTech.org, Top advertising & marketing news July 9, BestMediaInfo

AI Stack Daily

#Vendor & platform moves

  • Meta ships a reasoning image generator into the ad stack: New generation, editing, scene-redesign, and text-rendering capabilities rolling out across Facebook, Messenger, and Advantage+. Signal: creative production is being absorbed directly into the ad-buying platform. The walled gardens want the whole loop, ideation to creative to placement to measurement, inside their walls, which quietly raises the switching cost for anyone running creative outside them. Consent exposure (public IG images feeding both generation and training) is the regulatory tripwire to watch.
  • OpenAI full-duplex voice on GPT-5.5: Simultaneous listen/speak with reasoning and live web search, global rollout in ChatGPT. Signal: the assistant layer is becoming a viable front-end for commerce and service, which pressures brands to decide whether they show up as a skill/agent inside these assistants or get disintermediated by them.
  • Google Marketing Live (India) betas: Search, YouTube, Shopping, creative and measurement tools moving to market availability. Signal: Google is racing Meta to make campaign creation and measurement agent-operated. The category is converging on "describe the outcome, the platform assembles the campaign."

#Category watch

Retail media + AI-assembled campaigns: The global adtech market is ~$1.12T in 2026 (up from ~$987B in 2025), with programmatic, retail media, CTV, and AI-assisted campaign work the growth engines. The shift underway: retail media networks are bolting generative creative and automated measurement onto their first-party data, so the moat becomes data + automation together, not media inventory alone. Anyone building a martech org should assume campaign assembly is becoming a platform-native service, and plan to differentiate on data and measurement rigor rather than execution labor.

#Stack intelligence

The buildout is now gated at the hardware layer, and it's visible in the capital markets: SK Hynix's US listing ran ~7x oversubscribed on HBM (AI-memory) demand ahead of a Friday Nasdaq debut. For enterprise stack planning, the implication is concrete: model capability is outrunning the memory and compute supply needed to serve it at scale. Treat capacity and unit-economics of inference as a design constraint in any AI roadmap, not an afterthought, because the bottleneck is moving from "can the model do it" to "can we afford to run it at volume."

#Foundations concept of the day

Retail media network (RMN): A retailer selling ad placements against its own first-party purchase data, on its properties (site, app, in-store screens) and increasingly off-site. Amazon Ads is the archetype; Walmart Connect, Kroger, and even non-retail "commerce media" players follow the pattern. Why it matters at scale: an RMN monetizes something the retailer already owns (logged-in shoppers and real purchase history) at very high margin, and it gives advertisers closed-loop measurement (ad exposure tied to actual sales) that the open web can't match post-cookie. Example: a CPG brand shifts budget from open programmatic to a grocer's RMN because it can prove incremental sales lift against loyalty-card data, the same first-party-data advantage any brand with a logged-in customer base could build toward.

#Watch list

  • Assistant-as-storefront: With full-duplex voice assistants going mainstream, watch whether commerce and loyalty brands start shipping agent-callable skills. The brands that are agent-addressable will be reachable inside assistants; the rest get summarized about, not transacted through.
  • HBM/memory supply: SK Hynix's debut is a tell. Watch memory pricing and hyperscaler capex commentary next earnings season as the leading indicator of what AI features can actually ship at scale in 2027.

Sources: Latest AI-powered martech news, MarTech.org, AdTech market & news July 2026, bestmediainfo, Stock Market News July 9, Yahoo Finance

Markets Signal

#Macro pulse

Markets steadied and leaned green despite a second day of US-Iran strikes. USA: Nasdaq +0.6%, S&P 500 +0.3%, Dow ~flat, as the AI trade reasserted over war jitters (Wednesday's close was ugly: Dow -1.1% to 52,348, S&P -0.3% to 7,483). Oil: WTI +1.3% to ~$74.49, Brent +1.4% to ~$79.10 after fresh strikes (flagging: energy staying bid on Hormuz/supply risk, a persistent pressure on airline fuel costs). Canada: sustained crude strength is a two-sided pull for the loonie and TSX, supportive for energy names and CAD via the terms-of-trade channel, a headwind for fuel-exposed sectors like airlines. Asia: focus is on SK Hynix pricing its US offering today ahead of a Friday Nasdaq debut, AI-memory demand dominating regional sentiment.

#Today's industry move

SK Hynix's US listing is running ~7x oversubscribed on HBM (AI-memory) demand, pricing today for a Friday Nasdaq debut. It's the clearest capital-markets read yet that investors are paying up for the memory tier of the AI supply chain, not just the model layer.

#AI infrastructure watch

The bottleneck signal is memory. SK Hynix's oversubscription says HBM supply is the constraint gating AI buildout, more than raw GPU count right now. Combined with the recent Nvidia-nuclear moves on the power side, the pattern holds: the layers that determine what AI can do in 12-18 months (memory, power, cooling) are where the capital and the scarcity are concentrating.

#Signal or noise?

Signal: the AI trade absorbing a second day of Middle East escalation without breaking is a real tell about where conviction sits; energy staying bid is a persistent supply-risk repricing, not a one-day spike.

#Watch tomorrow

SK Hynix's Nasdaq debut Friday (pricing and first-day trade as a read on AI-infrastructure appetite) and whether oil holds ~$74+ into a third session.

Executive Pulse

#Macro signal

US-Iran escalation reprices energy risk: US forces struck Iranian targets late Tuesday after attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, and the President declared the prior US-Iran understanding "over." Oil surged ~5% to ~$74 WTI, equities sold off (Dow -1.1%, S&P -0.5%), and the chip complex extended its rout. Why it matters strategically: this is a supply-shock risk, not a demand story. Leaders should stress-test plans against a sustained energy-cost step-up and a stronger-for-longer dollar, both of which compress margins and consumer discretionary spend. For travel, marketing, and product leaders, the implication is to model a scenario where fuel and input costs rise while consumer demand softens, and decide now which investments are protected versus deferred.

#Tech industry

  • Chip selloff extends: Semiconductors continued to sell off, with weak Samsung earnings failing to steady the Nasdaq. Strategic implication: after a long AI-led run, the market is separating durable compute demand from priced-in optimism. Don't read a multi-day chip drawdown as an AI-demand reversal; read it as valuation gravity meeting a geopolitical shock.
  • Nvidia's energy strategy goes physical: Nvidia and nuclear startup Valar Atomics ran a Blackwell chip on power from an advanced reactor in Utah (July 1) and are weighing a 30MW near-waterless data center. Strategic implication: the AI leaders are now vertically integrating into power and cooling. Compute strategy is becoming energy strategy, and boards should expect capex conversations to increasingly include grid and generation.

#AI at the leadership level

The C-suite is consolidating AI authority at the top while adoption strains the org beneath it. Nearly three-quarters of CEOs now call themselves their company's chief AI decision-maker (2x last year's share), and firms expect to roughly double AI spend to ~1.7% of revenue. Yet 79% of organizations report adoption challenges (up double digits), 54% of C-suite leaders say AI adoption is "tearing the company apart," and only 29% see significant GenAI ROI (23% for agents). The governance gap is stark: only 38% of large firms have a Chief AI Officer, with no consensus on reporting lines. The pattern: ambition is centralizing faster than the operating model can absorb it.

#Leadership & org design

The CDO mandate is widening from data stewardship to human-centered digital leadership. A recurring 2026 move (Forbes profiled one this month) is retitling the CIO as CDO to emphasize the human connection to technology, not just the infrastructure. The durable insight for org-builders: the winning digital leadership role is being defined by adoption and change management, not tooling. The scarce skill is getting an organization to actually use AI well, not selecting the model.

#Question worth asking your team this week

If oil stays above $70 and the dollar stays strong through the quarter, which two AI investments do we protect no matter what, and which two do we defer, and can everyone in the room name the same four?

Practitioner Pulse

#Try this now

  • Artifact-first AI workflows: Stop letting decisions live in chat threads. Capture every design decision, eval result, and model choice as a durable record (a Markdown log, a registry entry, a shared Project). The teams doing this report faster handoffs and dramatically faster incident response, because the "why" survives after the conversation scrolls away. Set it up once this week: one shared doc per initiative that logs decisions with dates and rationale, not transcripts.
  • Persistent shared context over siloed prompts: Claude Projects, ChatGPT Projects, Google Gems, and Copilot Studio now let a whole team work against one shared memory instead of everyone re-priming a blank chat. The 20-minute win: load your team's real context (brand voice, current roadmap, key constraints) into one shared Project and make it the default entry point. It kills the "explain the background again" tax on every AI task.
  • The AI-native product loop: Reframe the product lifecycle from staged phases (research → plan → build → measure) to a continuously running loop where signals, opportunities, validation, and prioritization are always live. Practically: pipe product telemetry and support signals into a standing weekly synthesis rather than waiting for quarterly research. It compresses the distance between a user signal and a shipped response.

#Case study worth stealing

H&M, AI live-chat deflection: H&M cut customer-service operating costs an estimated 30% annually with an AI live-chat agent, while satisfaction (not just handle time) became the metric that improved. The steal for any digital org: measure your AI service rollout by CSAT and resolution quality, not deflection rate alone. Vendor-quoted deflection (70-80%) runs 30-40 points ahead of real enterprise medians (~41%), so anchoring the business case on satisfaction keeps you honest and keeps the rollout defensible when the vendor numbers don't materialize.

#Framework or mental model

Vendor-marketing delta: The structural gap between a vendor's cherry-picked case-study numbers and the cross-program aggregate you'll actually get. In AI customer service it's a 30-40 percentage-point deflection gap. Apply it to every AI tool eval: discount the headline metric by asking "is this a best case or an average?" and budget against the aggregate, not the demo. It's a cheap way to avoid over-promising to your own leadership.

#Rabbit hole (optional)

JetBrains' new "AI for Teams" (announced July 7) is worth an hour if you run an engineering-adjacent org: it's a vendor-agnostic layer that gives shared context, reusable agentic workflows, org-wide governance, and cost management over whatever AI tools developers already use, including long-running agents in managed cloud environments. The interesting pattern isn't the IDE features; it's that "govern and share the agents your people already use" is becoming a product category of its own.

Sources: The AI-Native Product Loop, Product Leadership, JetBrains AI for Teams, Team Collaboration Tools for AI Development 2026, MLflow, AI in Customer Service case studies, Cobbai, 59 AI customer service statistics, Zendesk

AI Stack Daily

#Vendor & platform moves

  • Salesforce → Informatica (~$8B): Salesforce closed its ~$8B acquisition of Informatica's AI-powered cloud data management platform (~$25/share, ~4.9x revenue on a mature ~$1.64B base). Signal: The CRM giants are buying the data-management layer, not just apps. Owning ingestion, quality, and governance is how they intend to feed agentic workflows. Data plumbing is now strategic real estate.
  • Adobe → Semrush (~$12/share, 77% premium): Valuing Semrush's ~108,000 customers at ~5.1x revenue. Signal: SEO, content intelligence, and creative tooling are converging into one stack. Adobe is betting that in an AI-search world, brands need content intelligence wired directly into creative production, not bolted on afterward.
  • Cordial launches AI-headless infrastructure: The enterprise marketing platform (Levi's, Tapestry, L.L.Bean, Boot Barn) now exposes every major platform capability as a service that AI agents can call and execute. Signal: "Agent-addressable" is becoming a platform requirement. If your martech capabilities aren't exposed as callable services, agents can't orchestrate them, and you're locked out of the automation layer forming above the app tier.

#Category watch

AI-native vs. traditional MarTech valuation split: The market is repricing the category in real time. Traditional martech traded at a ~7% discount to the broader SaaS M&A median in 2025 (3.8x vs 4.1x), while AI-native martech firms commanded 7.8x revenue, more than 2x the traditional multiple. The tell for anyone building a stack: acquirers are paying for AI-native architecture, not feature parity. Retrofitting AI onto a legacy platform does not earn the premium.

#Stack intelligence

Q1 2026 dealmaking cooled across adtech and martech overall, but the deals that did happen clustered tightly around three capabilities: incrementality measurement, identity resolution, and AI-driven performance optimization. That's the buy-vs-build tell for enterprise stacks right now. Measurement and identity are being bought (hard to build, trust-sensitive, standardizing), while performance optimization is where teams are still deciding. If you're building a martech org, treat identity and incrementality as procured infrastructure and concentrate internal engineering on the optimization layer that differentiates you.

#Foundations concept of the day

Incrementality measurement: The discipline of proving that a marketing action *caused* an outcome, versus taking credit for conversions that would have happened anyway. Last-touch attribution says "the ad got the click, so the ad gets the sale." Incrementality asks the harder question: run a holdout group that sees no ad, compare against the exposed group, and the *difference* is the true lift. It matters at scale because most attributed conversions are not incremental. A retailer running always-on branded-search ads may find that buyers would have found them anyway, meaning millions in spend is buying credit, not customers. Example: any large e-commerce brand can run geo holdouts, dark a channel in matched markets, and measure the revenue delta to size real contribution before renewing a budget.

#Watch list

  • Agent-addressable platforms: Cordial won't be the last. Watch whether the big CDP and marketing-cloud vendors ship "expose everything as a callable service" as a headline feature this quarter. It's the leading indicator of who survives the shift to agent-orchestrated marketing.
  • Data-layer M&A: With Salesforce buying Informatica, watch whether Adobe, HubSpot, or a hyperscaler responds with its own data-management or governance acquisition. The land grab for the layer beneath the apps is on.

Salesforce closed its ~$8B acquisition of Informatica (data management), and Adobe's ~5.1x-revenue Semrush deal continues to signal the SEO/content-intelligence/creative convergence. The market keeps paying up for the data and measurement layer even as broad adtech/martech dealmaking cools.

The energy layer is the story. Today's chip selloff is a valuation/geopolitics move, not a demand signal, but it widens the gap between infrastructure buildout (still accelerating) and equity sentiment (cooling).

Signal on oil (a supply-shock repricing that persists while Hormuz risk is live); mostly noise-plus-gravity on the chip drawdown (valuation reset meeting a risk-off shock, not a demand reversal).
